utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Popovic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. For the record, all the accused are present. The presentation is full house, except for Ms. Tapuskovic. Mr. Haynes, your closing arguments, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise if you can't see me clearly. I'm not sitting back here because the severity of this haircut won't stand too much close scrutiny. We've decided to stay here out of a sort of nostalgia, really. Having sat here for three years, we thought we'd finish here. A few months ago, when I opened this case to you, I underlined the themes that had been the Pandurevic defence and would continue to be developed during the presentation of his case. One theme was specifically not addressed; namely, that of his character. Neither was it developed in the course of the final brief. However, given the manner in which the Prosecution have addressed several issues in their final brief, it seemed to me only appropriate that I remind you of the substantial body of evidence within the case which placed the few matters relied upon by the Prosecution into their proper context. The matters I shall refer to in the following section of this closing argument derive entirely from unchallenged oral evidence and the testimony of witnesses admitted under Rule 92 bis without any requirement for their attendance for cross-examination. It can thus, I submit to you, be taken as unchallenged. Vinko Pandurevic was raised in a farming community in a multi-ethnic part of the former Yugoslavia. During his childhood, although aware of the different beliefs of his neighbours and school friends, he was brought up to believe in the principles of brotherhood and unity. It was the practice of his family to interact with their Muslim neighbours on their respective feast days, to respect their beliefs, and to cooperate in practical ways wherever possible. In the submission of the Defence, his upbringing and beliefs are of peculiar relevance in his case, informing, as they did, many of the decisions he was to take during the war in Bosnia. He entered service with the JNA through the Military Academy against his mother's wishes. It was the only practical solution to the funding of his higher and further education, as his parents had no money. Virtually all of his pre-war service, indeed virtually all of his adult life prior to 1992, was spent in Slovenia, where he settled with his young family and assimilated into local life and culture. There, he developed his interest in socialist politics. It was in Slovenia that he first commanded a unit. It was composed entirely of Slovenian conscripts. His commanding officer, Tihomir Blaskic, a Croat, became his best man or Kum. He learnt to speak Slovenian, contributed to local journals and magazines, came to regard the area as his home, and was loved and respected by his friends and colleagues there as much for his own ethnicity as for his endeavours to blend in locally. In considering his understanding of the situation of the ethnic communities Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well as his own personal beliefs, it is relevant, we submit, to remember that he had spent the 15 years prior to the start of the war outside Bosnia. After the commencement of hostilities in Bosnia, Pandurevic was deployed as part of a JNA unit in Visegrad. In spite of the occasional insinuation in this trial by the Prosecution about Visegrad, no evidence has been adduced, nor any suggestion made, which would cloud Pandurevic's reputation as a man or a soldier during this period. The Defence has adduced evidence, which will be referred to in due course, of actions which speak only of his positive qualities during that period. On the 18th of December, 1992, Pandurevic arrived in Zvornik to assume command of the Zvornik Brigade. He was a 33-year-old first-class captain. He was very young and very short of experience for such a role, especially given the size of the Zvornik Brigade, both numerically and geographically, which made it such a hard body to control. His effect upon the operative efficiency of the Zvornik Brigade was almost immediate. In truth, it had to be, because it and the region were in a pallor state of security at the end of 1992. Pandurevic tried to command the brigade pursuant to the rules and to the structure of the Zvornik Brigade as much as possible in accordance with military principles. He was perceived by his colleagues as a true or real commander. He was strict, but also correct and even-handed, so that other officers respected him and saw him as a real soldier. His strictness was based, first of all, upon strictness towards himself and then towards others. The discipline in the brigade was different when he was there, as opposed to when he was absent. Pandurevic treated all his soldiers equally, whether they were professional soldiers or not. As a commander, he showed neither favoritism nor prejudice. Milenko Jevdjevic recalled a combat situation when Pandurevic sent his own brother and his headquarters administration commander, together with Muslim porters who had work obligation, to take ammunition to units at the front. Milenko Jovicic described him more simply; he was just an extremely good person. A phrase from General Krstic's evidence was put to Pandurevic in cross-examination, where he was described as the best brigade commander in the Drina Corps, one of the best commanders amongst his peers in the army as a whole, a professional soldier in every sense of the word. He was equally respected by the civilian population in Zvornik. He was viewed as a very capable man of almost unique qualities, whose ability to solve a problem without raising his voice was well known. However, he was certainly not popular with the politicians or anyone in the political leadership in Zvornik municipality. His rating with them was not very good for all sorts of reasons, but mainly because he didn't let them interfere in the command of the Zvornik Brigade, something that they repeatedly tried to do, according to Miodrag Dragutinovic. He was, of course, an extremely effective combat soldier. Those who had the opportunity to work together with him in battle had a very high opinion of him as a professional soldier. They saw him as a young officer who, in the most effective way, put the knowledge he had gained in his military schools into practice very well during the war. He had a very high capability in the field of control and command of his units. He was capable of rapid planning, rapid deployment, and rapid implementation of an operation. Moreover, he had the skill to size up a situation, carry out preparations, and go into action in keeping with the situation on the ground, and he acted energetically. The Trial Chamber has heard at least three compelling examples of Pandurevic's skills as a commander in battle. These were, chronologically, Operation Mac 1, the taking of Ustipraca in June of 1993, the retaking of Zivko Brdo on the morning of the 10th of July, 1995, and the repulsion of the Croatian forces at Grahovo in the Krajina in August of 1995. These military successes were often achieved in spite of the poor quality of the units under his command or the tactical ineptitude of his neighbouring units. The Trial Chamber will doubtless have got the impression that whoever he was dealing with, Pandurevic was not a man who suffered fools gladly, and moreover he was never afraid of speaking his mind. The Trial Chamber may or may not conclude that in describing some of the non-governmental organisations present in Republika Srpska as good-for-nothings - Prosecution brief 1311 - this aspect of Pandurevic's character was well reflected. Nonetheless, throughout the entirety of the war, Pandurevic's relationship with international organisations was constructive and cooperative. His assertion that as a soldier he was primarily interested in peace is credible and borne out by evidence of his behaviour. His pride in his relationship with General Morillon, a witness on his 65 ter list, in the spring of 1993 was plain. Pandurevic complied with the general's requests and ensured free movement and free passage for General Morillon while he was carrying out his duties as a UN commander. His orders to the members of his unit as to how to deal with members of the Dutch Battalion during Krivaja 95 were entirely proper and completely unchallenged. He was an active participant in the execution of the Dayton Peace Accords between November 1995 and his departure from Zvornik, cooperating both with IFOR and the Bosnian Army forces. In spite of his youth and inexperience, Pandurevic was neither afraid to question orders which were, in his view, unjustifiable, nor to act on his own initiative. He showed that not just on the 11th of July in Srebrenica and in Bratunac, we maintain, nor just on the 16th of July in Baljkovica, but throughout the war whenever the situation demanded. The Defence invite the Trial Chamber to view that in the case of Pandurevic, actions truly speak louder than words. In the submission of the Defence, Pandurevic's actions in July 1995, in standing up to Mladic and contravening his orders to destroy the column were neither isolated nor borne of necessity, but were, rather, the concrete expression of his character and integrity through his actions. To that end, the evidence of Pandurevic's actions prior to the critical events of July 1995 is more than mere character evidence. The types of evidence envisaged as being relevant to culpability in the prior jurisprudence of this Tribunal do not fall into this category. In those cases, it amounted to no more than evidence of a lack of prejudice or general good character. The episodes about which this Trial Chamber has heard during the course of this case relate directly to the question of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for slowing down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: -- propensity and state of mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, you're being invited to slow down a little bit for the sake of the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I will. The episodes about which this Trial Chamber has heard during the course of the case relate directly to the question of propensity and state of mind. Where there is an issue, for example, as to the motivation of the accused in letting the column pass at Baljkovica, the Defence contend that it is relevant to take into account the fact that on prior occasions Pandurevic behaved in a precisely similar fashion, when neither he, nor his forces, were at any risk. I'm going to list now just a few of the episodes of Pandurevic's behaviour which we will ask you to take into account in determining his motivation and state of mind in July of 1995. In April of 1992, in Visegrad, Pandurevic protected Muslim civilians from Serb paramilitaries, disarming the latter and forcing them to return to Serbia. He also provided food to the Muslim population and pledged to protect them; that this may have been a piece of evidence which went unnoticed. It derives from 7D1191, the 92 bis witness statement of Guso, Midhat, and I will read from it: "Soldiers of the Uzice Corps of the JNA Yugoslav National Army asked locals to declare arms in their possession. They came up to my house. They did not go inside. One of the soldiers started as if he were to enter the house and began to act in a rough manner. Another soldier then approached him. He did not allow him to go inside, saying, 'Act decently or I will report you to Vinko.' When I heard the name Vinko, I did not know who that referred to. I assumed that it was a reference to an officer who does not permit violent and arbitrary conduct towards Muslims. At that time, I did not know Vinko Pandurevic. I saw him for the first time two or three days after the event that I recounted. I note that the unit under Vinko Pandurevic's command had kitchen at the house of one of my brothers, where it prepared food for the troops. Pursuant to Vinko Pandurevic's order, the food from that military kitchen was distributed also to us, residents from the village." He goes on at paragraph 11 to say: "In view of the circumstances, it is my belief that the members of this paramilitary group would have killed those of us standing around the post office but for the fact that Vinko Pandurevic prevented them from doing so." Shortly after becoming commander of the Zvornik Brigade, Pandurevic established contact with the commander of the opposing forces, the ubiquitous Semso Muminovic. They quickly established a hot-line, their contacts led to regular prisoner exchanges, an agreement on the shelling of certain inhabited areas, an agreement for cease-fire of sufficient duration to permit each side to sew and reap crops bi-annually. On the first occasion of such a cease-fire, the arrangement was almost entirely to the benefit of Muslim forces, who were under attack by Croat forces and facing famine, again a piece of evidence that might have escaped your attention, so I'll read from it. It's 7D1191, the 92 bis witness statement of Semso Muminovic: "At that meeting, I explained to Vinko Pandurevic the difficult situation we were then facing due to lack of food. At that time, Muslim forces were engaged in a conflict with the Croat Defence Council. For that reason, the delivery of food supplies from Tuzla was difficult. A food supply crisis appeared imminent, affecting both civilians and army personnel in that area. I suggested a truce to Vinko Pandurevic in the duration of one month to allow the spring harvests preparations to be made. By truce, it was understood that there would be no shelling of inhabited or uninhabited areas or roads; in other words, that there would be a complete cease-fire. In response to my proposal, Vinko Pandurevic said that he did not have his command's approval, but that regardless, he would agree to the proposed truce on his own responsibility. He said, 'Semso, the truce is in effect from the day after tomorrow at noon. Let the people work in the fields, whatever may happen to me.'" In late January of 1993, Pandurevic made an arrangement for the daily passage of Muslims at or near Kamenica. The arrangement allowed for those who were trapped by combat to pass safely. During Operation Mac 1 in June of 1993, Pandurevic's unit, through the efficiency of its actions, trapped several thousand Muslim forces at Ustipraca. They had advanced far more rapidly than their neighbouring units, and because of the dominance of the position they had taken, the Muslim forces were completely at their mercy. Notwithstanding this and completely without the authority of his superior command, Pandurevic allowed all soldiers, civilians, vehicles, and arms to leave the area, in quotations "without a single bullet being fired." This was done at the initiative of Pandurevic by direct communication with the opposing commander, Ahmed Sejdic. These last two incidents will be returned to in greater detail in due course, as the Prosecution brief has confused the two episodes in its submission. The unanimous experience of those who worked with Pandurevic as a commander was that his treatment of his and his instructions as to the treatment of prisoners of war was at all times consistent with the Geneva Conventions. Upon his return to Zvornik on the 15th of July, 1995, his orders that prisoners were to be kept alive at all costs were well known. Symbolically, when, on the morning of the 16th of July, a Muslim communications officer was interrogated by his chief of staff, that man had his wounds treated, was fed, and released safe and sound. Moreover, on the 18th of July, a group of seven to ten Muslim teenagers was at the 4th Battalion command post tasked by somebody to dig fortifications.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for reading slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Haynes, my attention has been drawn to ask you to read more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Pandurevic immediately told these men to stop digging, ordered Dragan Jokic to guide them through the minefield to the safe Muslim side, and contacted Semso Muminovic and told him he was sending the teenagers back to him. He was to call Pandurevic back and let him know if they had arrived safe and sound. In due course, he did so. It is well documented that a large number of prisoners arrived at the Batkovici camp in the latter half of July 1995. They came from the Zvornik Brigade detention facilities. Moreover, it is plain from the evidence that Pandurevic was active in securing their transfer to that place for exchange. During the course of this trial, a number of witnesses have expressed their view as to the effect which Pandurevic's absence had during the crucial periods of the indictment, upon unfolding events. Perhaps most graphically, Lazo Ristic said: "I'm still not clear why this was done in Zvornik when our commander was absent, and in a way it so happened that they came through the command of our battalion, where the commander was also absent. If they had been there, I believe that things would not have happened the way they did." As an example of the command culture within the Zvornik Brigade, it should be remembered that Lazar Ristic, who spoke elsewhere in his evidence about the guiding example of Pandurevic's command, withdrew his men from Orahovac when he discovered a murder operation was in process. As was developed in our brief, it is not merely Pandurevic's absence from Zvornik during the critical days of July and September of 1995 which is important. Of equal if not greater importance is his absence from the taking of crucial decisions; for example, the decision to transfer prisoners from Bratunac to Zvornik for execution, taken on the evening of the 13th of July, and the decision to disinter and rebury bodies buried in the Zvornik area, taken sometime in late August or early September of 1995. Pandurevic's absence from Zvornik at those times and from those decisions making processes was accidental and enforced. It was, however, well known to those involved in taking those decisions. Now, I have taken some little time in outlining this evidence to you because, in our submission, it goes directly to six issues raised in the Prosecution brief. It goes, firstly, to the question of the credibility of Vinko Pandurevic as a witness. It goes, secondly, to counter any suggestion that this is a man who has ethnic bias. It goes, thirdly, to illustrate the reality of the command climate that existed within the Zvornik Brigade. It goes, fourthly, to illustrate the way in which he and those subordinate to him habitually treated prisoners of war. It goes, fifthly, to the question of how you weigh up the evidence concerning his actions in allowing the column to pass on the 16th of July. And it goes, lastly, to the question of genocidal intent, given the way in which the Prosecution have put its case in that regard. We submit that if you give proper weight to the evidence I've outlined in this short section of these oral arguments, that you will reject many or all of the Prosecution's submissions about Pandurevic in those six regards. Now, to switch horses for just a moment, I would like to take just a few moments to analyse the purpose of this exercise. This is, in truth, a sweeping-up operation. I have been putting the same case for three years, as I think everybody recognises. I'm not going to repeat it all today. However, I wish to make a few observations. Pandurevic's case was plain from the cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses. The themes we have developed could not have been clearer. Pandurevic appeared as a witness on his own 65 ter list filed in April of 2008. His was the last case, and accordingly by the time he gave evidence, the areas where he contradicted other parties' cases had completely crystallised. The Prosecution case does not meet Vinko Pandurevic's case, nor even comment upon it, in a number of very material respects. To give some of the starkest examples of where the Prosecution does not comment, either in its final brief or its closing submissions upon the case for Vinko Pandurevic, I'll pick just four: One, that Pandurevic had no effective control of the Zvornik Brigade between the 4th and the 15th of July, that this is an evidential, not a legal consideration, and you'll find not one submission in the Prosecution brief addressed to that issue. Two, the legal status of the Yugoslav National Army brigade rules, a theme we developed in great detail both during evidence and in our submissions, not one comment. Three, the allegation that Pandurevic returned to Zvornik on the morning of the 12th of July, something which PW-168 was effectively commissioned to say during his evidence here, but not a theme developed in the Prosecution brief at all. And, four, the biggest gaping absence of all, not a word about the zone of responsibility on which so much of the Prosecution's case hinges. We were laughed at, frankly, for causing PW-168 to sit there with enormous maps and join the dots and explain that the Prosecution zone of responsibility theory was nonsense. To find not one word addressed to that issue in the Prosecution brief is startlingly surprising, to say the least. We submit boldly that where the Prosecution does not deal with issues such as this, raised by the Defence throughout the trial and in its brief, to which the Prosecution has the right to reply in its oral arguments, as a matter of natural justice, those issues simply have to be resolved in the favour of the defendant or the accused. But matters don't stop there. In opening this case, I specifically challenged the Prosecution and all parties to put their case to Vinko Pandurevic when he gave evidence. I made a bit of a joke about it at the time, aligning the practice of putting your case to my Englishness, but it's not an English thing; it's in the Rules of this Tribunal. It's Rule 90(H)(2), and I don't imagine you need reminding of that. But what Rule 90(H)(2) says is: "It is in the cross-examination of a witness who is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party, counsel shall put to that witness the nature of the case for the party for whom that counsel appears which is in contradiction of the evidence given by the witness." You may think that in the case of an accused giving evidence on his own behalf, the Rule has particularly sound reasons. Firstly, that you, the Trial Chamber, are entitled to see the reaction of an accused to an accusation put to him. Secondly, you're entitled to see his answer. And, thirdly, that everybody accused of criminal behaviour is entitled to have an opportunity to answer the accusation which is a central part of the Prosecution's case. The Prosecution, itself, agrees that the Rule is important and criticises, I think, most of us for failures at some stage during the case to challenge one thing or another with odd witnesses. But given especially that Pandurevic gave evidence as the last substantial witness in the Defence case and that, as the Prosecution have acknowledged, there was no stopwatch on cross-examination, the issues were absolutely crystallised. There is simply no excuse for failing to put to him significant aspects of the Prosecution case. We have analysed closely the allegations now made in the Prosecution's final brief and contrasted them with the cross-examination of Vinko Pandurevic. The Prosecution's final brief is simply replete with assertions that were not put to Pandurevic in cross-examination. We simply don't have the time to list them all, but where relevant as we go through the relevance, we will highlight assertions in the final brief not put to Pandurevic in cross-examination. For present purposes and simply to highlight the evil in this, I'll illustrate that to you with three examples. The first: In paragraph 1537 of the Prosecution's brief, the Prosecution avers that the performance of the reburial operation on the 27th of September is also consistent with the Zvornik Brigade's use of an unusually large amount of D2 diesel on that date, 3.870 litres, without any description in the daily combat report of legitimate engineering works in the Zvornik Brigade zone of responsibility. This is, indeed, an apparently compelling point and one which might suggest that the reburial operation was in full swing on the 27th of September, and that Pandurevic could not have failed to know about it. However, the document upon which this assertion is based bears a little closer analysis. And I'm not going to call much into e-court during the course of these submissions, but I will call this. It's 7D681, and we'll need to look at paragraph 6, please. Thank you. At paragraph 6, as you'll see, records in standard pro forma terms consumption, and every regular combat report has that at paragraph 6. Let us all agree that 3.800 litres is a lot of diesel to consume in one day. Indeed, it's probably far more than ten digging machines operating all day could consume. But let's look at paragraph 6 a little more closely. It seems that on that day, diesel was not the only commodity that was being excessively used. If 3.800 litres of diesel is a lot, 12.600 7.62-millimetre rounds is the sort of amount of rate of ordinance discharge you would have expected on the Somme in 1914. It's massive. A thousand 12.7-millimetre rounds, 320 30-millimetre rounds, 20 122-millimetre shells, 10 130-millimetre shells. We submit that that level of use of fuel and ammunition cannot possibly reflect the use of materials on the 27th of September. So what does it mean? The answer is: I don't know. But if this document had been put to Pandurevic when he gave evidence, and it had been suggested to him that this amount of fuel had been used for reburials on that day, he might have been able to explain it. He might, for example, have said that sometimes under paragraph 6 the brigade told the corps command what it needed. If this document had been shown to PW-168, he might have been able to say that this fuel and ammunition related to the fuel and ammunition required by the 2nd Drinski Brigade which left for the Krajina the day before, the 26th of September. If this document had been put to Sreten Milosevic, the assistant commander for logistics, responsible for such matters, he might have offered yet another explanation, perhaps that the amounts were what the brigade had in stock. But this document was shown to nobody by the Prosecution. It was simply used as the basis for a submission in their final brief. And we submit that the inference they require you to make or invite you to make in the circumstances is simply impermissible. A second example of a matter not being put: In paragraphs 1340 to 1343 of the Prosecution brief, the Prosecution makes, apparently, four assertions: One, that members of the Drina Wolves were in Potocari; two, that those members of the Drina Wolves were part of Tactical Group 1; three, that they were under the command of Vinko Pandurevic; and, four, that they would have reported back to him what they saw in Potocari. It's clear, the answer. Not one of those propositions was put to Pandurevic when he gave his evidence, not one. Had they been, who knows what he might have said. He might have said, I took a roll-call of my men on the 12th of July, and they were all there, so these people couldn't have been from Tactical Group 1. He might have said that Krstic had asked him for two or three men to be at his disposal on the morning of the 12th of July in Potocari, and these were them. But we'll never know because it was never put. The evidence in the case is that the Drina Wolves were a unit comprising about 360 men. You'll get that from P382. The evidence is absolutely clear and unchallenged. They were in the Drina Corps unit under the direct command on the 12th of July of General Zivanovic. In July of 1995, various elements of the unit were deployed in the Sarajevo theatre - see footnote 567 of our brief - and with Tactical Group 1. About 120 of them were part of Tactical Group 1. By necessary inference, a number of them were not deployed at all on the 12th of July. There simply is no evidence that even if there were odd members of the Drina Wolves in Potocari on the 12th, that they were under Pandurevic's command or that they were the Drina Wolves that were part of Tactical Group 1. Under the principle that the senior officer present is in command of a mixed unit, then Mladic must have been in command of what was going on in Potocari, or Krstic at worst. As to the suggestion that the Drina Wolves were in Potocari, in our submission, it doesn't make any sense. You don't send your elite fighting unit to take part in crowd control. The units that were in Potocari were security officers and police units, not fighting units. Self-evidently, Pandurevic wasn't in Potocari, himself. So how could they get their orders from him if he wasn't there? Moreover, there is virtually nobody who is not on some piece of film or still photograph. Potocari was filmed from a number of sources and perspectives, and had there been any Drina Wolves members, they would have to have been on films or photographs. Again, the failure to put this suggestion or these suggestions to Pandurevic simply makes it impossible for you to draw the inference, adverse to him, that these men were Drina Wolves, were from his unit, were under his command, and would have reported to him. It's a complete false theory. The third suggestion which I raise by way of an example appears in paragraph 1337 of the Prosecution's final brief. That reads as follows: "Pandurevic's admission that units under his command, as opposed to the units from the 2nd Romanija Brigade or the 1st Birac Brigade, took the features around the town of Srebrenica, and ultimately the town itself is significant, because the UN's Bravo Company compound and the Muslim population in it were shelled at around noon on the 11th of July, injuring several people. Pandurevic knew that these indiscriminate shelling attacks were occurring and were carried out by the units under his command." This assertion is bordering on the outrageous. Nothing of this was put to Pandurevic. Had it been so, he might have been able to explain that the timings were all wrong, that his units didn't take the surrounding features until much later in the afternoon, that the town by then was empty, that his artillery units had been withdrawn somewhere else, or just simply that it is not true, that he didn't know these things, that units under his command did not shell Compound Bravo. There is simply no basis for even inviting this inference. In the circumstances, and I do not apologise for taking some little time with these three examples - I can't do it with every one of them - but as we go through the evidence I will be inviting you to the view that where an accused has given evidence on a particular issue and the Prosecution fails to challenge it, he is entitled and the Trial Chamber is entitled to regard that as uncontested, and assertions in the final brief by the Prosecution on matters which haven't been put to Pandurevic ought simply to be disregarded. Unless that is the consequence on the breach of the Rule, there is no point in having the Rule at all. The evidence of Vinko Pandurevic stands to be judged by exactly the same standards as that of any other witness. I don't say that to insult the intelligence of professional judges, but he is no more and no less credible by reason of his standing accused on this indictment. In paragraph 1279 of the Prosecution's final brief at the foot of page 362 and going over to page 363, there is an assertion by the Prosecution which purports to be supported by legal authority. Whilst the Defence accept that the Prosecution is perfectly entitled to invite the Trial Chamber not to believe the accused on some or all of his evidence, to submit that the Trial Chamber should not do so as a matter of law, where it is uncorroborated, is not only wholly disingenuous, it's irresponsible and incorrect. It is, of course, the law in many jurisdictions that an accused's evidence against a co-accused needs corroboration, but the decision in Delalic was based on its own particular facts; in particular, that the accused concerned who gave evidence had a mental state that was seriously in issue. And to invite you to extend that principle to the lengths that it is suggested in paragraph 1279 is quite wrong. Pandurevic's credibility is for you to judge. You saw him and heard him, and you are able to judge whether his answer on any given issue is both truthful and reliable. And we do invite you to look again with care at his evidence and, in particular, the answers he gave in cross-examination, in detail. His evidence is substantially consistent with all the other evidence in the case, leaving aside most notably, perhaps, the evidence of PW-168. It is a central irony of this case that some of those who question his credibility concurrently present cases which necessarily involve them alleging that 8, 10, or 14 witnesses, including their former colleagues and friends, have conspired to lie about them, that documents which implicate them are forged, and that their unwittingly captured radio conversations were either incapable of capture, were mis-transcribed, or are now misconstrued. Little wonder that the inconvenient evidence of Pandurevic against them is added to their conspiracy theories. Pandurevic's evidence is heavily relied upon both by the Prosecution and other parties in this case. Listing every footnote would be boring, but we invite you to note how frequently his evidence is said to be truthful in different parts of both the OTP and other Defence briefs. Pandurevic's evidence involved giving details of events which he was not compelled to do by the Prosecution case and which might have been taken to be incriminating. To give you a few examples: That soldiers under his command were responsible for the taking of UN observation posts; that he met and spoke to General Krstic on a number of occasions, not proved as part of the Prosecution's case; that he learnt of the reburial operation shortly after his return to the Zvornik Brigade in late September; that these, we say, supplement and support his general credibility. Please also remind yourselves of the points we made in our final brief as to his credibility, about his stance on intercepts, contemporaneous documents, and the general conduct of his case. Paragraph 1279 of the Prosecution brief, after misrepresenting the law, as we have submitted, on the treatment of the accused's evidence, goes on to list a series of what I will call areas of dispute in the case between the Prosecution and Pandurevic, which it terms deliberate falsehoods. The Defence cautions strongly against the approach advocated by the Prosecution. The Trial Chamber, of course, knows that these are the points where the Prosecution and the Defence disagree. That does not make them deliberate falsehoods. These are the issues for you to decide. We reiterate the points that by giving his evidence, the Prosecution's burden of proving their case and, at the same time, disproving his evidence, is the harder. It is not a deliberate lie to say you disagree with the Prosecution case. Now, an extraordinary amount of time has been devoted by the Prosecution, in its final brief, to 1993. At what relevance those passages and further submissions made the other day by Mr. McCloskey have is unclear. At paragraph 1281 of its final brief, the Prosecution state that its case does not depend on Pandurevic's role in the VRS campaign in 1993. It goes on to say, however, Pandurevic spent a significant amount of time testifying about his participation in these events, misrepresenting his role, and putting forward a sanitised and misleading version of events. It concludes by saying that the materials set forth in paragraphs 1282 to 1312 demonstrate his lack of credibility as a witness as well as his knowledge and intent with respect to the charged JCEs. On the face of it, the only issue all this material could go to, it not being part of the Prosecution case against Pandurevic, is to his credibility. However, we're not naive. Directive 4 and the Spring Offensive has always been at the heart of the Prosecution's case, and to suggest that Pandurevic would not have been cross-examined about it, had he not raised it first, is unworthy of a straightforward prosecutor. Apart from anything else, Pandurevic's role in Kamenica and Konjevic Polje was first put to a witness in June 2007 by the Prosecution and raised in detail with Milenko Jevdjevic two months before he testified. We will now briefly address those allegations in this part of the Prosecution's brief. Paragraphs 1285 to 1288 discusses the issue of Kamenica. Kamenica was not part of Pandurevic's case from the beginning. You can see that from the 65 ter summaries served in his case. No reference was made to it in the opening of his case, and certainly at no time have either he -- has either he or I described him as the hero of Kamenica. The evidence about Kamenica came out as a result of the Prosecution's cross-examination of Milenko Jevdjevic at T-29718, which the Defence then tidied up in re-examination by putting into evidence the regular combat report 7D1006. This was a month before Pandurevic commenced to give evidence. The matter having been raised in that way, it was inevitable that Pandurevic would deal with it in his own evidence and explained what happened. Kamenica has been fundamentally misunderstood by the Prosecution. This was not the passing of a column such as took place, for example, in Baljkovica. This was an arrangement for a daily passage along a safe corridor. There is abundant evidence that at the time of this operation, Kamenica itself was uninhabited and had been for some time, and you can find that at T-12803, the evidence of Miodrag Dragutinovic, and T-0799, the evidence of Vinko Pandurevic. Read chronologically, the problems with the passage of lost people across a combat zone first came to Vinko Pandurevic's attention on the 30th of January, 1993, and you can see that from the document put to him, P4233. As a result of that, a radio announcement was made, and he announced directly to those who wished to cross the combat zone that they could do so between certain hours of the day. You will get that from P4229 and 7D1006, the regular combat report for the 1st of February. You will note that that document was dispatched at 11.40 in the morning. At 9.00 that night, General Zivanovic sent a report from the corps to the Main Staff. He announced that he had taken the decision to create a safe passage. That, in fairness, was put to Pandurevic when he gave evidence. It wasn't a document that he had written, but he came up with the obvious explanation, that he reported to General Zivanovic what he had done and General Zivanovic then took upon the decision for himself. The chronology makes that perfectly logical. By contrast, the incident at Ustipraca five months later has been part of the Defence case from the very outset, and you will see that from our 65 ter list. The episode which Pandurevic relied upon in his evidence as illustrating an identical situation to that he faced at Baljkovica was the safe passage allowed there. This incident was described in great detail by four witnesses: Pandurevic, himself; Dragica

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: (redacted). Pandurevic, himself, wasn't challenged about his actions at Ustipraca. Thus, it was never suggested to him that he had ever been anything other than truthful or accurate about these events. When you read or re-read the Prosecution's final brief about the events of 1993, you will find not one word about Ustipraca. It has simply been ignored. And the Defence submit that it is deliberately ignored, Ustipraca, and deliberately sought to confuse you by confusing that with the episode of Kamenica which it raised and pursued. It cannot be an accident that the former is referred to so often and the latter not addressed at all. That is because we submit that the Prosecution is fully aware that Pandurevic's behaviour on that occasion is a highly relevant and pertinent consideration in your concluding how to determine his actions at Baljkovica. Paragraphs 1289 to 1297 deal with allegations that in the early spring or perhaps late winter of 1993, Pandurevic was responsible for shelling Muslim civilians. We make four brief points: Firstly, that every document referred to in those paragraphs references mixed military and civilian targets; P409.70, referenced by Pandurevic in his own evidence, deals with the legality of mixed military and civilian targets and attacks upon them; thirdly, the recording of these events accurately stands to Pandurevic's credit, not to his demerit; and, fourthly, the fact that the Drina Corps removed references to civilians from its own reports is, frankly, irrelevant when considering Pandurevic's intentions or credibility. At paragraph 1295, an episode at Konjevic Polje is raised. We would point again simply to four matters. The reference in the report in paragraph 1295 is to civilians being caught in the fire. There is an obvious inference from that that civilians were not the target of the fire. Secondly, it is not a proper inference to draw that a unit under the control of Pandurevic fired two isolated shells after 1530 in the afternoon. Three, the report 5D1323, relied upon by the Prosecution, is dated the 15th of September, 1993, eight months after the incident described. The entire document describes military operations between January and August 1993, without any specification as to dates. There is no evidence that it is referring therein to the incident of the 12th of February covered by this instant and this passage in the Prosecution's brief. And, fourthly, in spite of his own evidence, the evidence discloses that once contacted, the shelling did stop. Paragraphs 1298 to 1306 of the Prosecution's brief deal with allegations relating to the burning of Muslim villages. We submit that the suggestion that Pandurevic's troops burned houses is based on the most tenuous evidence imaginable. He has described in great detail the military campaign that he participated in during this period. He has denied that his units burned houses or destroyed mosques. The evidence that someone else reported to General Zivanovic that houses were burning on his particular axis of attack, and that the Zvornik Brigade cleared away an already-destroyed mosque one year after the event, doesn't get close to surmounting that evidential obstacle. There is no evidence of the destruction of habitat in any areas where Pandurevic was principally involved. Kamenica, Konjevic Polje, self-evidently, since he was active in preventing it, Ustipraca, Visegrad, Zeleni Jadar, Zivkovo Brdo, Rajna, Bojna, all the areas where you have heard he carried out combat operations, there is no evidence of the burning of any habitat. And don't you think there would have been some evidence if those things had happened? As to the relevance of these events, over and above a challenge to his credibility, we submit that the Prosecution position is illogical. Just because an accused has the temerity to explain his involvement in events he would undoubtedly be cross-examined about doesn't make them relevant to establishing his participation in one or both of the alleged JCEs. The obvious corollary would be if he stayed silent about these matters, they wouldn't be relevant, and that can't be correct. I confess to this day I am still not clear where it is that I will find the alleged illegal purpose of Krivaja 95. It has been variously suggested to exist in the six strategic goals of May 1992, Directive 4 from November 1992, Directive 7, Drina Corps Operational Directive 7.2, and the combat order itself. I must be going very fast. In our submission, it is unthinkable that a court would determine the individual criminal responsibility of a soldier, professional or otherwise, by reference to the political doctrine or strategic objectives of his native country, especially those espoused at the start of ethnic conflict or at the height of the violence between two communities. To do so would come preciously close to finding that all Serbs had and continued to have throughout the duration of the war the common intent to commit genocide and/or crimes against humanity. Moreover, to rely upon the utterances of government or strategic command from 1992 ignores all temporal considerations. It is as if two years didn't happen, there were no cease-fire agreements, no peace negotiations, the international community was not involved, there were no periods of peace, there were no flagrant breaches of the terms of the agreements by the enemy which more immediately necessitated the operation with which we are concerned. It also completely ignores the reality of the situation in Bosnia in 1992. The Prosecution perennially speaks in its final brief and in its submissions of a brutal campaign in 1993 or a violent VRS campaign. The beginning of this war was violent. We will concede that. But this Trial Chamber only has the sketchiest details of the combat in Podrinje from the start of the war until the campaign which concerns this trial. The Prosecution really only want you to consider one period, one part, and one side of the conflict. They ignore the evidence such as 7D1124, 7D1125, 7D946, 7D968, 7D965, 7D992, and 993, which set out, as it were, the violence which was committed upon the Serbian community by its enemy. Pandurevic described his whole war, including all the military operations he took part in. These were classic military operations, and he is not charged with any crime against humanity or war crime in relation to them. The problems created by the Prosecution's dual goals or twin objective theory lies first, as I have already said, in divining their derivation. Are they derived in 1992 or are they derived from the documents of 1995? We submit that some -- the idea of some over-arching objective on which the combat plan was based, taken to its logical conclusion, would mean that quite literally nobody subject to it could act lawfully. If, for example, the determining document is said to be Directive 7, then every Drina Corps soldier, going about his daily business, would have been doing so with the ancillary intention of making life unbearable for the inhabitants of the enclaves. Imagine this: One day, you are manning the lines, doubtless thereby effectively tying down enemy resources, the next, with a stroke of General Miletic's pen, you're a party to forcible transfer merely by doing the same thing. The combat order Krivaja 95 does not, in fact, express more than one objective, we submit, rather than express the same objective in a number of ways; we suggest four: One, separation of the enclaves; two, reduction of the enclaves to their urban areas; three, creating conditions for the elimination of the enclaves; four -- I'm sorry, I'm going too fast again. Thank you. The urban area is not defined, but the extent of the military objectives is defined. For example, Tactical Group 1 had to achieve Zivkovo Brdo, so if you look at the detailed objectives of the combat order, it would still leave a substantial area easily sufficient for the population to live in. Thus, the Prosecution assertion of that the objective of reducing the enclave in size was intended to cause a humanitarian disaster and, thus, criminal, is a false assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Haynes, did you say the fourth objective?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll have to come back to that. Thank you. Also, the phrase "elimination of the enclave," paragraph 4, is ambiguous, and it is not safe to assume that it meant forcible transfer of the population rather than neutralisation of the 28th Division as a military force. Apart from anything else, it doesn't make sense to say "reduce in size and create conditions for its elimination" if your objective is so to constrict it that everybody would have no choice but to leave then. It is plain that what is meant is to create a new perimeter which is easier to police and stop excursions by the ABiH into Serbian territory, because, necessarily, the smaller the perimeter, the less soldiers you need to guard it, thus you would eliminate the enclave as a military feature, not as a place for people to live. We're bound to observe, in relation to the case of the dual goals: Firstly, that the way in which the Prosecution's case is put in this trial is inconsistent with the way it was put in Blagojevic and Krstic; see Krstic at para 136 and -- sorry, Krstic, para 199, and Blagojevic, 136. Secondly, the VRS force wasn't sufficient to achieve the illegal objective as alleged. Even the Prosecution contend that any one of the number of factors occurring would have stopped the illegal objective from being achieved, Naser Oric being there, the 28th Division putting up a proper fight, Clear Skies on the 11th of July allowing NATO to drop bombs on Serbian forces, et cetera. Thirdly, when Pandurevic departed to the operation, he expected nothing to come of it, and that, we say, is proof of his intentions. Fourthly, when he achieved his objective under Krivaja 95, namely, the taking of Zivkovo Brdo, he and his forces withdrew, and his evidence is that he expected to go home. And lastly but not leastly, he was a tactical commander whose concerns were local, and insofar as the orders from above were concerned, were specific. In relation to the dual goals of Krivaja 95, the Trial Chamber has visibly been concerned with where you draw the line, and it received some assistance on that point from Mr. McCloskey the other day. It is interesting to see whether their theory as to that bears out any careful scrutiny of the way in which this case is now put, and the Trial Chamber might briefly like to consider how the indictment is framed in deciding where you draw the line between those who are participating in the joint criminal enterprise forcibly to transfer the population and those who are not. The Prosecution contend, at paragraph 1620 of its final brief, that Pandurevic was in a precisely similar position to the tactical commands of other brigades, in particular Mirko Trivic and Svetozar Andric, and certainly it is true all of them took part in Krivaja 95 and all of them are brigade commanders. All of them commanded units which attacked Muslim forces at Srebrenica. All of them entered Srebrenica town. All of them were present at a meeting at the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade, whenever that took place, and all of them marched towards Zepa. Trivic and Andric took part in the assault on Zepa between the 14th and the 24th of July. Trivic and Andric had units in Zepa throughout that period, and they also, if you have regard to Trivic's diary, P4309, took part in the loading of civilians onto buses. Self-evidently, neither of them have been indicted. And more importantly, if you have regard to paragraph 97 of the indictment, the only brigade commanders listing as participating in a JCE are Pandurevic and Blagojevic. Moreover, in paragraph 98 of the indictment, Trivic's unit, the Romanija Brigade, is not even listed as a participating unit in the implementation of the JCEs. When Trivic testified, the Prosecution was specifically asked by His Honour Judge Kwon at the start of his testimony on the 18th of May, 2007, whether a Rule 90 warning should be given to him, and the Prosecution said, in clear terms, one was not necessary. That's at T-11793. So the Prosecution's position is, necessarily, that, in particular Trivic, and by necessary inference Andric, are guilty of no criminal behaviour. They were not part, apparently, of a joint criminal enterprise forcibly to transfer, that neither had the intention for forcible transfer, neither aided and abetted in forcible transfer. In short, neither is guilty of any criminal behaviour at all. Given their identical roles and their presence at the alleged crucial meeting in Bratunac, where is the line of distinction now between Pandurevic and Blagojevic and the other two? The answer, in our submission, is perfectly simple. Criminal liability in this case has got nothing whatsoever to do with knowledge of the legality or otherwise of the Krivaja 95 operation. It has nothing to do with whether you had seen, read, or considered Directive 7, nothing to do with whether your units encountered DutchBat on the outside of one or other of the enclaves, nothing to do with whether you saw or participated in the evacuation of the civilians. The sole determining factor as to whether you, as a brigade commander, are deemed criminally liable for participation in the JCE to forcibly transfer civilians is whether prisoners ultimately die in the municipality where your command post was based. And that may be a convenient moment to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This may be bad news for the interpreters, but I do need to speed up a little bit. I'm going to move quickly on over a couple of topics I was going to cover to that event and directly to the area which may cause me to be accused of unmitigated arrogance. I'm going to deal with the question of the meeting at the Bratunac Brigade. This is dealt with extensively in both our brief and the Prosecution's final brief, but just a few points, please. Firstly, Trivic's diary and his evidence are not independent evidential sources. They stand and fall together. And if you needed a transcript reference for that, it would be T-11978, where Trivic, himself, concedes that point. There are, we submit, a number of compelling reasons as to why Trivic's recollection and recording of the meeting on the 12th of July simply cannot be right. There are seven. Firstly, according to his recollection, there were no prisoners in the center of Bratunac on the evening that he attended a meeting. Secondly, there was no information at the meeting he attended about the whereabouts of the 28th Division. Thirdly, that on the afternoon or late evening of the 11th of July, General Mladic, as we saw on the video, had been exhorting all his officers, Trivic included, to go to Bratunac that evening. It only makes sense that they would. Fourthly, there were no buses in Potocari when Trivic passed through it on the evening he went to the meeting, only people. That can only have been the 11th, not the 12th. Fifthly, during the meeting Mladic received a telephone call which Trivic overheard relating to the provision of fuel for buses. This is directly sequential to the conversation Mladic had had with Karremans at the first Hotel Fontana meeting about the provision of transport and fuel for the evacuation. No such conversation could have taken place on the 12th of July. Sixthly, Trivic's evidence was that the conversation he overheard was Mladic arranging the commencement of transportation from Potocari the following day. That's at T-11980 to 981. That night, he saw no buses in Potocari. And, seventhly, Trivic said in evidence that he passed through Potocari again on the day after the meeting he had attended in the afternoon, and he then saw large crowds of people being loaded onto buses. The evidence from DutchBat officers is that the evacuation was completed by about 5.00 p.m. on the afternoon of the 13th. Accordingly, there could have been no large crowds there on that afternoon for him to see. The diary itself, we submit, is ambiguous as to the date. And for the second time and possibly the last time, I'm going to call a document into e-court. It's already on the screen, and in particular the passage relied upon by the Prosecution in its final brief needs your attention. It reads: "By 8.00 tomorrow, General Kostic," that must be Krstic, "must prepare a decision for the liberation of Zepa." And continues further down: "In the morning of the 13th of July, at 10.00, General Mladic will personally address the soldiers in the vehicles sector at the line reached." What is significant about this record is, firstly, that Trivic has recorded an order by Mladic to Krstic to produce not an order, but a decision by 8.00 the following morning. The Prosecution have conveniently overlooked that fact in linking this diary entry to the production of the order for combat produced by Krstic on the 13th of July. However, the more logical link between what is written here and subsequent events is that Krstic arrived at a decision by 8.00 on the 12th and then went to the Bojna repeater at 9.00, where he met the commanders and announced his decision to sweep the terrain towards Viogor prior to the action in Zepa commencing. Secondly, and we submit significantly, why Trivic would have recorded in the very next entry that Mladic would have addressed the soldiers at 10.00 on the 13th of July, rather than "tomorrow," makes no sense. The use of the phrase "the 13th of July" in that entry plainly implies that the following day was not the 13th of July. Most of the other evidence touching on this meeting has been substantially reviewed in the briefs, and I'm not going to go over it again. However, two additional pieces which require, I submit, your attention: Firstly, the evidence of Miodrag Dragutinovic. His evidence, we submit, is doubly relevant because he said not only that Pandurevic told him on the 12th that the meeting had been on the previous evening, but also that, critically, at 5.00 in the afternoon of the 12th, when Krstic, as we know, went to Viogor to meet the commanders, Krstic told him that Mladic would come the following day to address the troops. Krstic could not have known that if Mladic only said that at a meeting five hours after he spoke to Miodrag Dragutinovic. Therefore, Krstic must have known that from a meeting which took place the previous evening. I know it's been a very long trial, but you might remember Miodrag Dragutinovic, the operations officer from the Zvornik Brigade, a chartered surveyor by profession, a small, measured, and quiet man, who probably gave some of the most reliable and credible evidence that the Trial Chamber's heard in three years, in our submission. He was called as a Prosecution witness. They didn't have to call him, but they did. And to suggest now, again without any contradiction of his account during re-examination which was then permissible, that he is lying, that, we submit, is inappropriate and incorrect. He had been the subject of a 146-page interview. They knew what he was going to say, and he was not challenged about it, and was called as a witness of truth. His re-examination went on for several hours and was even adjourned overnight. Again, no suggestion made that he was anything less than honest or accurate about the date he recalled being told by Pandurevic a meeting had taken place the night before and, by Krstic, that Mladic would come the following day. The second point really arises directly from that, which is, I think we all agree, that on the early evening of the 12th of July, Krstic did go to Viogor and he did speak to all of the brigade commanders who were going to go on to Zepa. That, in our submission, makes a nonsense of the idea that all of those people then went from Viogor back to Bratunac later that evening to discuss, doubtless, precisely the same thing. Now, there has been a lot of discussion about the date of the meeting, but almost none about its content. The Prosecution's approach seems to be that proof of the date is sufficient and the rest can simply be inferred. Whatever was the date of the meeting, it is actually instructive to look at who was not there. Beara wasn't there; Popovic wasn't there; Kosoric wasn't there; Tolimir wasn't there; Momir Nikolic was nearby, but he wasn't in the meeting; Vasic was not there. Nobody from MUP was there. And who was at Potocari? Well, most if not all of the above. In our submission, the meetings which can be proven to have taken place at around this time indicate clearly where the division of function lay between the soldiers and those concerned with prisoners. The people at this meeting were the military men, whose responsibility would be to defeat the ABiH at Zepa, i.e., to fight. These were not the men whose concern, under the combat order or generally, was the taking or detention of prisoners or the movement of civilians. The Prosecution say, Why would Mladic conceal these things from his military commanders? We say the counter argument is: Why would he tell them? He had mobilised and ordered the relevant people and resources to deal with Potocari, and he didn't need his military commanders to do anything or know about it. The evidence as to separate meetings with security men in this case is a bit vague, but those people didn't all appear in Potocari by magic, so there must have been separate meetings and it must have been before the bussing of the population at Potocari began. It's illogical to infer that the same matters needed further discussion with people who were about to be dispatched to fight in Zepa. Quite simply, the argument doesn't work. They did not need to know. Leaving aside the physical circumstances which, of course, would suggest that Trivic is wrong, the Prosecution's assertion about what the commanders must have known by the 12th of July are based exclusively on the evidence of Momir Nikolic, which the Prosecution itself has conceded cannot be relied upon where not corroborated by other reliable evidence; paragraph 502. His assertions, moreover, as to what he told Blagojevic are completely without corroboration. Accordingly, the Trial Chamber should, on the Prosecution's own invitation, regard its submissions about what Pandurevic must have known even if he had attended a meeting on the 12th of July. Lastly, a submission which I've briefly touched upon, the position of Trivic himself, not said to be part of a joint criminal enterprise, not necessary to give him a warning under Rule 90 before he gives evidence. It is now suggested in the brief that he not only took part in a meeting at which forcible transfer and murder was discussed, in spite of his denials, but, moreover, that he has committed perjury on that subject. We say to make that suggestion at this stage is outrageous. I'm going to move on now to the sections of the Prosecution brief which deal with my client's alleged knowledge of the murder operation, and I'm going to start with the 13th of July. Firstly and foremostly, there is no doubt or dispute that between the 12th and 13th of July, Pandurevic was moving from Viogor towards Vlasenica. You might recall that on the late evening of the 13th of July, we find him refueling his car in a convoy at a petrol station in Vlasenica. He did not encounter any Muslim forces. Nobody suggests that he did. There were no Muslim forces in the area through which he was passing, though -- thus, there is no question of him being aware, in his immediate vicinity, of the taking of any prisoners. There's no evidence of any communication between him and anybody in Bratunac, and there's absolutely no reason why he should have got in touch with anybody in Bratunac. The Prosecution's submission that the movement of prisoners from Bratunac to Zvornik was due to the presence of NGOs and international agencies is completely false. There is no evidence that that was the motivation for moving the prisoners. Deronjic's evidence is that the prisoners were moved quite simply because he demanded it. In fact, the murders at Kravica, just outside Bratunac, on the main road, Cerska, and the Jadar Valley, if the Prosecution's theory is believed, completely destroy the notion that anybody was worried about outside agencies. If further confirmation were needed that the theory is nonsense, even after the decision of Karadzic and Deronjic to move the prisoners to Zvornik, Beara was still looking for places to murder them in Bratunac on the morning of the 14th, so he plainly didn't care who might see him doing it. The Prosecution theory that the decision to murder all the men was taken sometime on the 12th depends entirely on the evidence, we submit, of Momir Nikolic. Again, the Prosecution say of him, where his evidence is not corroborated, you should not rely upon it. We say that that is not correct, and the evidence does not support any such finding, and the matter is dealt with fully in our brief. It is correct that Mladic addressed the troops on the morning of the 13th of July and that Krstic was there with him, but there is no evidence that he talked to Pandurevic or anybody else, for that matter, about the plan to murder prisoners at that stage. And the Trial Chamber has heard not only from Pandurevic, but also Trivic and Dragutinovic, and no suggestion was made to them that any such information was passed. At that stage, the morning of the 13th of July, the decision to move prisoners to Zvornik had not been taken, so there was no need to make Pandurevic a unique recipient of such information. The idea that Mladic would share all his plans and the activities of his chief of security with a load of brigade commanders involved in combat is ridiculous and not supported by any evidence. The decision to move the prisoners from Bratunac to Zvornik was taken at a high political level, and it was taken swiftly. The Prosecution's concession at paragraph 1392 that it is unclear whether Pandurevic knew that the prisoners were to be moved to Zvornik, can only be read as an admission that there isn't sufficient evidence to find that he did. All the evidence, we'd suggest -- we'd submit a number of things. Firstly, that the decision to move the prisoners was taken at 8.30 on the 13th of July. Secondly, that within a very short time Drago Nikolic was informed, probably by a call from Popovic, though the Prosecution's position on that is far from clear. Thirdly, that Beara didn't want to move the prisoners and that even the following day he was trying to find a way to kill them in Bratunac. And, fourthly, while all this was going on, Vinko Pandurevic was marching towards Zepa. There is no evidence that anybody contacted Pandurevic, and why would they? Firstly, if the Zvornik Brigade commander needed to be warned to get ready for some prisoners, the person to tell was Obrenovic, who was in command of the Zvornik Brigade on the 13th of July. Telling Pandurevic, who was on a completely different mission, marching towards Zepa, was out of radio communication with the brigade, would be practically useless. Secondly, the last thing Beara wanted was another municipality telling him he couldn't kill his prisoners there. He wanted this over and done with quickly and efficiently. Accordingly, the evidence that Pandurevic knew depends exclusively upon PW-168's assertion that Drago Nikolic told him that Pandurevic knew. That would necessarily depend on some contact being made with Pandurevic on the march, between the time when the decision to move prisoners was taken in Deronjic's office and the time when Drago Nikolic was called, but neither Deronjic, nor Beara, had the means to contact Pandurevic from the SDS office, and Momir Nikolic for sure did not do so. Even from the Bratunac Brigade Command, there is no evidence that Pandurevic was even contactable whilst on the march. It is significant throughout these days that when he received orders from Krstic, he received them face to face at meetings. PW-168's evidence on this point is probably untrue. It's designed to minimise his own personal responsibility. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: (redacted) or that Popovic lied to Nikolic. In any event, it is impossible to conclude, as the Prosecution very nearly concedes, that Pandurevic knew of the plan to move prisoners to Zvornik on the evening of the 13th of July. Going over to the 14th, there is no evidence even that Krstic knew, by the 14th of July, that prisoners had been taken to Zvornik, and there is no reason that he should have been told, because even adopting the regular chain of command, Beara had no duty to report to Krstic, Deronjic had no military duty at all and certainly none to report to Krstic, and Momir Nikolic had no duty to report to Krstic. As I've already said, we submit that the Prosecution's warning as to the testimony of Momir Nikolic means that you cannot even find that he informed his own commander, because he's the only source of evidence for that. So on the 14th, in the morning, at Krivace, Krstic could not even have told Pandurevic about the movement of prisoners to Zvornik. Moreover, there is no evidence that anything about prisoners was said at that meeting on the morning of the 14th. Again, Pandurevic gave evidence about that, as did Trivic, Jevdjevic, Dragutinovic. All were at Krivace on the morning of the 14th at the time the combat orders for Stupcanica 95 were given out, and no suggestion was put to any of them that prisoners were discussed. We submit it cannot be inferred, contrary to the direct evidence of Pandurevic and these other four witnesses, that the Prosecution's case is correct and that information about prisoners was passed that morning. Assuming the contrary, however, and that Krstic was aware by the morning of the 14th that prisoners had been moved to Zvornik, and that he did inform Vinko Pandurevic of that, what is, therefore, remarkable is that at that time there is no communication between Pandurevic and the Zvornik Brigade. Of that, we can be absolutely sure, because if there had been, PW-168 would for sure have told you. The duty operations officer's notebook would have recorded it, and there would probably be an intercept. That would surely have been the time to get in touch with his command if he had been told about the arrival of the prisoners. It's simply inconceivable that if he had been told by Krstic on the morning of the 14th of July about the movement of the prisoners that he would -- about the movement of the prisoners to Zvornik that: one, that he would not have know about the column; two, he would not have contacted the brigade; and, three, he would have taken up his positions in Zepa at all as if nothing had happened. Again, at paragraph 1392, the assertion that by that time the murder operation was clear to everyone derives solely from the evidence of Momir Nikolic, and on the Prosecution's own invitation, should be disregarded. Let's move forward to the morning of the 15th, please. The Prosecution claims at paragraphs 1270, 1393 to 1398, that Pandurevic had to know or needed to know about the murder operation in order to fight the Muslim column effectively, and Krstic simply must have informed him about this before his return on the 15th of July. We have a very great number of submissions to make about this, indeed 13. Firstly, nobody suggests that the danger which the column represented to Zvornik was known before the evening of the 14th of July. The Prosecution do not even -- do not even suggest that, even at the morning of the 14th, Krstic would have talked to Pandurevic about the column or its dangers. So what other operations were going on in Zvornik which Krstic made and probably didn't know about had no impact. Secondly, the murder operation was a Main Staff security operation being carried out by security officers and military policemen from the Main Staff, the Drina Corps, and the Bratunac Brigade. There is no reason a brigade commander should be told about it. Thirdly, as we have demonstrated, there is no such thing as a brigade zone of responsibility, so the fact that the prisoners were taken to the municipality of Zvornik had nothing to do with Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: (redacted). According to PW-168, he had no idea that the Zvornik Brigade resources were involved in the killing operation, that is, apart from Drago Nikolic, five military policemen and two digger drivers. They would have had no impact whatsoever upon the brigade's combat capabilities. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Fifthly, by the early morning of the 15th of July, the information was no better. Especially bearing in mind that the last contact with Obrenovic had been on the evening of the 14th, there was no information that there was a difficulty with guarding, killing, or burying the prisoners available at the command post on the morning of the 15th. Sixthly, if Obrenovic thought that the resources being used to guard prisoners were compromising the brigade's combat capability, he would have said so in his report on the 14th of July or at least during his conversation with Jevdjevic the night previous. Seventhly, as to the Zvornik Brigade resources and the allegation in paragraph 1397 of the Prosecution brief that significant numbers of Zvornik Brigade resources were being used up, the amount of resources committed to guarding prisoners in digging graves peaked at 50 on the 14th of July. During the course of the next few days, it dwindled. The Zvornik Brigade had five and a half thousand men at its disposal. Fifty is less than 1 per cent of the brigade's manpower. Not every battalion was engaged in active combat on the 14th, 15th, or 16th of July, and you had the opportunity to see the quality of some of the men who gave evidence in this case, and I mean them no disrespect, but, for example, those from the 1st Battalion, who came to speak to you and told you about standing guard, unarmed, in the vicinity of their local school. Do you seriously think that their absence from the front-line made any difference to the Zvornik Brigade's fighting capability? Eighthly, the telegrams from Obrenovic and the other sources which were available to Krstic and Pandurevic on the morning of the 15th of July made no reference to the killing operation. Ninthly, the intercepted telecommunications on the morning of the 15th of July between Pandurevic and the brigade command would negate any suggestion that Pandurevic had just been informed of the killing operation in Zvornik. It is inconceivable, we say, if Krstic had just told him that there were all sorts of problems arising from the killing operation occurring in Zvornik and that resources were having to be committed to it from the brigade, that Pandurevic would not have asked about it, even in cryptic terms, when he called Mijatovic and Milosevic on the morning of the 15th. If, as the Prosecution say, he needed to know from Krstic, he so much more needed to know from Zvornik Brigade members what was going on on the ground, and a commander like Pandurevic would for sure have inquired about that issue if he knew there was an issue. Tenthly, Dragan Jokic, according to the Prosecution's submission the other day, is a weak man. I don't know about that, but one thing I do know is he's a very careless user of the airwaves. You need look no further than his intercept with Colonel Beara on the evening of the 14th of July at 2102 - 1164 - or his conversation at 9.39 with Bratunac Brigade Command at 9.39 - P1176 - where he was effectively told to shut up rather than give away the whereabouts of his commander on the air, but when Dragan Jokic spoke to Pandurevic on that morning about whether there were any problems, he said nothing. Now, that may well mean that I'm making a point in Colonel Beara's favour, because that may well mean that when he referred to problems the night previously to Colonel Beara over the radio waves, he was, in fact, referring to the column and nothing else. But for sure having his commander on the line, it is a stark surprise that he, Dragan Jokic, doesn't say anything which Vinko Pandurevic couldn't have prevented him from saying. Eleven, we all know now that we can add up the men and machinery that, in fact, were involved in Orahovac and Petkovci, but nobody knew then and certainly nobody had knowledge then of the sort of numbers that the Prosecution now allege were involved. Twelfthly, if Krstic told Pandurevic about the killing operation and the involvement of the Zvornik Brigade in the morning, why didn't Krstic then tell Beara when he called him at 10.00 that morning, a few minutes later? Beara was complaining that he had problems. Surely, logic dictates, if Pandurevic was in the loop of knowledge, that Krstic would say to Beara, Pandurevic is on his way back, knows about everything. Why don't you take a few of his men, hey, perhaps from the 3rd Battalion? They're not involved in combat. If Pandurevic had been part of or knowledgeable of the killing operation and knew about the involvement of the Zvornik Brigade, there is no way Beara would not have asked for resources from the Zvornik Brigade for executions in the Zvornik area. There is no way that Krstic wouldn't have told him Pandurevic was returning. The only reason that Beara did not seek help from Pandurevic was that Pandurevic was not part of the plan. This intercept is perhaps as critical as the combat report of later the same day in understanding the evidence that there is and there is not against Vinko Pandurevic. We say it is the clearest illustration that at that point in time nobody could possibly infer that he had any knowledge that the operation was going on. Thirteenth and last, if Krstic spoke to Pandurevic on the morning of the 15th about the fact that the killing operation had been moved to Zvornik, why would Pandurevic, ten hours later, write him a report telling him about the prisoners in the schools? That would effectively be Pandurevic writing to Krstic to say, Hey, Krle, you know those prisoners you told me about this morning and the problems we've got with them. You're absolutely right, we have. We submit that the whole Prosecution theory about what Pandurevic would have needed to know and, therefore, must have known from his meeting with Krstic that morning is utterly false and is based upon inferences that you cannot possibly draw when you look at the evidence in the round. We do add, yet again, that this is a case where the direct testimony in the case from Jevdjevic and Vinko Pandurevic, as well as the hearsay evidence of Mijo Dragutinovic, completely rules out any such transfer of information at that stage. Now, one of the great mysteries of the case, if you accept Pandurevic might be right as to how he came progressively to know about the executions in Zvornik, may be why Dragan Obrenovic did not tell him sooner. It is a perfectly valid question. They had been colleagues for two and a half years and worked closely together. They had mutual respect for each other. You would expect Obrenovic to tell Pandurevic at the first available opportunity. So why didn't he? Well, let us not lose sight where the burden of proof lies in all this.
