This, perhaps more than any other episode in the case against Pandurevic, is one where I have to remind you that it's for the Prosecution to prove beyond reasonable doubt that he did, and we submit, in any event, that PW-168's uncorroborated evidence alone on this topic does not discharge that burden. The history and the impossibility of PW-168's corridor story and conversation is dealt with extensively in our brief as well in the brief for Drago Nikolic. In reality, the Prosecution is left with nothing else to hold their case together on this topic than to cling desperately to the notion that Pandurevic had to know about the security threat and that Obrenovic had no reason to conceal this from his commander, but let's analyse it. The following are a series of operating factors upon Obrenovic which may act exclusively of each other or, in certain circumstances, in combination. Firstly, if PW-168's evidence about Obrenovic's conversation with Drago Nikolic is true, then Obrenovic would have believed that Pandurevic was already fully informed and, accordingly, he had no need to know, least of all in front of an assortment of policemen he had never met before. Secondly, conversely, it is possible that he had nothing to tell. The precise details of Obrenovic's state of knowledge of the murder operation and who was involved in it by the 15th of July, at about midday, is almost impossible to be sure about. At the bottom end, he might have known no more than that Drago Nikolic wanted to be relieved from the IKM and needed five military policemen to secure some schools. At the other extreme, he might have been fully aware of the murder and burial of prisoners at Orahovac and Petkovci. The truth is almost impossible to work out, as even the Prosecution concede. Accordingly, what, in fact, he knew at noon on the 15th of July, if not very much, he may not have thought worth telling Pandurevic about -- he might not have thought worth telling Pandurevic about, given the urgency of the military situation. In any event, he may not have had the opportunity. Even in his 2001 interviews, Obrenovic made a point of saying that he wanted to report to Pandurevic. At that time, of course, he was asserting only about the military situation, but that he didn't get a proper opportunity. Pandurevic simply came into the office on the 15th of July. Obrenovic briefed Pandurevic for 15 minutes, and then Obrenovic was sent off to his task. This version of how the meeting on the 15th of July was conducted, whatever the state of Obrenovic's knowledge, is remarkably consistent with all the evidence we now have available. And why would he have lied about that in 2001? Fourthly, he may have been afraid to tell Pandurevic what he had done, or at least have wanted the possibility of time to think best how to explain himself. Obrenovic was in the Command of the Zvornik Brigade on the 13th and 14th of July. He made the decision to relieve Drago Nikolic of his post as duty officer and provide him with five military policemen. He authorised the use for two excavator operators for burials at Orahovac. Obrenovic may have been more seriously involved than that. We just don't know. He very well may have feared that Pandurevic would disprove his actions, whatever they may have been, and criticise them. Fifthly, whilst Obrenovic told Pandurevic of the conversation with Drago Nikolic, he did not do so, on any version of events, until more than 24 hours after Pandurevic's return. This is curious. There, of course, remains the further possibility that the conversation was made up by Obrenovic in the first place, but, more importantly, that shows that there must have been a second conversation between Pandurevic and Obrenovic where Obrenovic revealed the genesis of his information; i.e., the number of prisoners, the involvement of Zvornik Brigade machinery, whose orders they were following, et cetera. And it may well be, as I've already said, a combination of all those five reasons. The fact of the matter is you simply cannot infer that the conversation did take place because there is no sensible explanation as to why it wouldn't. We suggest there are several explanations as to why it wouldn't, and we've listed them there for you. In truth, to approach it in that way, as Mr. Josse was addressing you about at length on Friday, is a classic case of reversing the burden of proof. It is for the Prosecution to persuade you that PW-168's evidence is truthful and reliable, and not for Pandurevic to persuade you to the contrary. He merely has to cause a doubt to be cast on that evidence. Given that the Prosecution, as we will submit in due course, have abandoned as truthful several important areas of PW-168's evidence, two of the most important examples being Pandurevic's presence in the Zvornik Brigade on the 12th of July and the meeting with Popovic, we submit, on the 16th of July, it is the Defence submission that you cannot rely upon his evidence as credible or reliable in this respect. I'm going to turn now, as quickly as I may, to the irregular combat report of the 15th of July. In brief, we submit that the Prosecution's analysis of this document is neither objective nor logical. The Prosecution's case as to the meaning of this document is circular. The argument goes: The report, itself, is evidence of his knowledge, and because of his knowledge, you can, therefore, interpret the document adversely to him. The interpretation, we say, is based upon a number of false assumptions. The first is that enormous or tremendous resources of the Zvornik Brigade were engaged in dealing with prisoners. They were not. That is simply false. Thirty, forty, or fifty men was a drop in the ocean and wouldn't have made any difference to anything. Secondly, that Pandurevic knew that the murder operation was in progress, that prisoners were awaiting executions, and that Zvornik Brigade resources were involved in these operations, there's no evidence that he did, and it all depends on who told him. If he is or might be right that the only information he had prior to writing the report came from Brano Grujic and Ljubo Bojanovic, then he had and could not have had the information that executions were taking place and that the Zvornik Brigade was involved. Thirdly, that the situation on the ground was accurately reported in the first five paragraphs, it wasn't. The best example, perhaps, is that the report suggests that the numbers of the column which -- I'm very sorry, I'll start that again. The situation on the ground was not accurately reported in the first five paragraphs of the report. Evidence suggests that the numbers of the column which eventually did walk to safety were far higher than those mentioned by Pandurevic in the report. And fourthly and perhaps most significantly, that by the time he wrote the report, Pandurevic's position was that he would allow the Muslim civilians to go free, but not the soldiers. In truth, by the evening of the 15th of July, the only sticking point was whether they could take their arms with them or not. This is doubly significant, firstly, because it completely negates the Prosecution's baseless suggestion at paragraph 1443 of its brief that Pandurevic was fully ready to destroy the army and, secondly, it adds real significance to paragraph 6 of the report, the one that reads: "I have made an offer to the commander of the opposite side," et cetera. This paragraph foreshadows the report on the 16th of July in which Pandurevic said it was possible that some soldiers got out with the civilians. The obvious inference is, if he had already decided they could all go by the time he wrote this report, then that is what he was referring to when he said, Let them go, and it has a direct correlation with its report of the following day. A few further observations on the report. The assertion of the Prosecution made in paragraph 1449 quite simply should be disregarded and cast to one side. Pursuant to the practice, as pointed out to Mr. McCloskey when he was putting to General Pandurevic the opinion of Mr. Radinovic in another trial, then unless adopted by him, none of that has the force of evidence, Mr. Radinovic's opinions in the Krstic case, whether read into the record of this case or not, simply should not have found their way into arguments in the Prosecution brief. None of what he says has the force of evidence, particularly when denied and disagreed with by Vinko Pandurevic. In relation to paragraph 1445, the suggestion that the additional burden is not based on any knowledge of Pandurevic about trouble in the areas, we say only this: He had been the Zvornik Brigade commander for two and a half years, he was very well acquainted with the way in which battalion soldiers would react and, in particular, what was likely to make them desert their posts or refuse to go to the lines. There is a stack of evidence from Pandurevic, PW-168, and Dragutinovic about the occasions in when this happened during the course of the preceding three years, and Pandurevic would know what the incipient dangers of prisoners in schools, near to prisoners' homes, were. He didn't have to have direct knowledge of any particular complaints. The reliability of Eileen Gilleece's note as a piece of evidence was specifically dealt with in our brief, and very little more needs to be said. In reality, the Prosecution want to accord the Gilleece note with the status of a suspect interview, and we submit it cannot be regarded as such. In virtually all jurisdictions in the latter half of the 20th century to date, it was recognised, through advances in technology and the rights of the accused, we needed to protect people in interview situations so that courts could be sure that anything said in an interview situation was both accurately recorded and related to answers given in a satisfactory situation; voluntariness, I suppose, is the key to it all. The Gilleece note fails on all counts. No suspect should be interviewed in these circumstances, and no record of this sort ought to be used to contradict him as to the detail of what might have been said. We are absolutely sure that Ms. Gilleece, in creating this note, did not envisage that it would end up being used for purposes other than that for which she intended it; namely, to provide a brief note on the gist of her lengthy conversation with General Pandurevic. The Prosecution have simply not grasped the point which Pandurevic made about pigs when he gave evidence. What Pandurevic was saying was that Richard Butler was interpreting the word "asanacija" far too narrowly by merely translating it as burying the bodies. Therefore, Pandurevic used the example of pigs to show that the word means more than that. He was not saying that the reference to "asanacija" in the irregular combat report of the 15th of July was a reference to the pigs of the 16th of July or the pigs of 1992. He was saying that on those occasions when that happened, the clear-up of the mess was "asanacija." In many ways, the passage relied upon in the note displays the danger of using it as a verbatim record of the conversation. According to Ms. Gilleece's note, they were talking about a report from 1992 involving the 4th Battalion. Pandurevic's immediate explanation, not ultimate, that the discussion covered both the 1992 and 1995 pigs, makes perfect sense of the record and cannot simply be dismissed. In relation to the note concerning the information he received from the chief of staff about the presence of prisoners in Zvornik on the 15th of July, two mistakes are equally possible. Firstly, that the translation of the position of the man who informed him is inaccurate or, secondly, that the date is wrong. Significantly, Ms. Gilleece records nothing in her note as having happened on the 16th of July, which is inconceivable, because it was the 16th of July that he let the column go at Baljkovica. Where she got it wrong, we don't know, but get it wrong, she did. It is correct to say that in paragraph 1456 of its final brief, the Prosecution identifies six areas where Eileen Gilleece's report records events accurately, but what should not be forgotten is that the evidence is that at least part of the discussion was conducted by reference to a copy of Richard Butler's report. History, I'm afraid, does not relate which of his reports they had before them, but even a cursory glance at his narrative report of 2000 would reveal references to Drago Nikolic and the office he held - at page 19 - his replacement by Major Galic at the IKM on the 13th of July - page 98 - and the taking of 23 prisoners by the Zvornik Brigade on the 22nd of July - page 83. Gilleece's note, as we pointed out in the examination of the accused, is notably more accurate where there is a text for her to refer to. In any event, some accuracy in the note doesn't prove its entire accuracy, and the Defence stands by its position that, as a record, it is incapable of effectively contradicting Pandurevic's evidence about the important events of 1995. Lastly, nothing personal was, in fact, intended. It is the use of the record as a means of contradicting direct evidence which we criticise, not Ms. Gilleece. However, describing her as professional in the circumstances of this interview is, we submit, a bridge too far. On the evidence, she broke many rules in the conduct of this interview, and apart from anything else, this is one of those curious areas where there is direct evidence in this case on the topic. You might remember I asked Dean Manning what he thought about conducting interviews while everybody was drinking alcohol, and he said, at T-19150, that that would be thoroughly bad practice. The Prosecution asserts in its final brief, without any evidential basis whatsoever, that the words "terena" and "teritorija" are entirely different phrases. The evidence is at T-31001 and T-32640, quite to the contrary, that these two words are synonymous. However, one thing we can agree on; searching the terrain and "obezbedjenje terena" are self-evidently different things. Even the Prosecution would agree with that. So the submission in paragraph 1447, that Pandurevic had already referred to "obezbedjenje terena" in paragraphs 1 to 3 of the report is palpably wrong, even on their own interpretation of these phrases. I'd just briefly like to revisit the "let them go" issue, and really make this submission: The idea that Pandurevic could have let the prisoners of war go and chose not to do so, on the evidence you have heard, is ridiculous. Firstly, for a start, by the time he got back to Zvornik, most of them were dead. Secondly, he didn't know where they were. Thirdly, these prisoners were being held under the orders of General Mladic, the VRS commander-in-chief, who himself had been present on the ground on the 14th of July and had dedicated his chief of security to the whole operation. Fourthly, all levels of the army were involved, multiple units from the Main Staff, the corps, and other brigades; also, private companies and municipal organs. The Prosecution agreed with this picture of events. It is fanciful to suggest that a 35-year-old, red-headed youngster could have gone to any of these killing sites, even if he had known where they were, and could have got there in time, and simply let the prisoners go. I'm going to leave the topic of the report because I'm running out of time rapidly, but I do say that there's no compromise on this. The report of the 15th of July is a difficult document to interpret. The Prosecution acknowledged it's a difficult document to interpret. Richard Butler has gone through the whole spectrum of interpretations of this document, and I know that you find it difficult to interpret. Everybody has been troubled by this. But unless you can be satisfied that all the adverse inferences that the Prosecution wish to you draw are the only interpretations of this document, you have to resolve it in favour of the accused. There's no ducking the issue. If they are not inferences which you think are the only inferences you can draw and the only interpretations of this document, then it becomes wholly exculpatory of Vinko Pandurevic. And we submit that when you do look at all the surrounding evidence, what he could have known, what he could have done, that that is the only choice faithful to the burden of proof you will apply, that you can come to. Now, I'm going to leave that and move on to the question of command of the killing operation, and I'd like, really, to highlight for you what I submit is a symbolic and important paragraph in the Prosecution's brief, and it's paragraph 1468. And I'm not going to dwell on it to any great degree. Why it is symbolic and significant is that that is the first time, chronologically, in the whole history of events where you will find any allegation in the Prosecution's brief that Pandurevic had effective control of any units or elements of the Zvornik Brigade. Symbolically again, we say that when you analyse Mr. McCloskey's closing remarks the other day, he talked about General Pandurevic assuming responsibility when he returned on the 15th of July. Now, if you read it as a piece, it will be plain to you that despite the absence of detailed submissions, the Prosecution do not concede the question of de jure command. They contend that during this period, Pandurevic remained de jure command in the absence of a formal replacement, and you'll find that at paragraph 1618 to 1625. So the concession must be taken, we assume, to be to the effect that Pandurevic was not a de facto commander of the Zvornik Brigade from the 4th to the 15th of July, and you may think that's a perfectly reasonable concession on the evidence. This, we submit, marks a "volte-face" from the position the Prosecution took at the start of the case. They have specifically, we say, abandoned the following positions: One, that Pandurevic returned to the Zvornik Brigade Command on the morning of the 12th of July and had a conversation with Dragan Obrenovic - you'll remember that well; two, that he had any meaningful contact between -- sorry, that he had any meaningful contact with the Zvornik Brigade Command between the 4th and 15th of July; and, three, that he commanded the units prior to his return. If that is right, and we submit your driven to that conclusion from the absence of any arguments to the contrary in the Prosecution brief, as well as the evidence, then two things must follow: Firstly, that he can have had little or no knowledge of the precise deployment of elements of the Zvornik Brigade when he did return; and, secondly, that there was no need for him to know anything of the murder operation in Zvornik on the 13th or 14th of July, for sure, because he could have no effect upon it. We acknowledge, as is alleged in paragraphs 1469 to 71, that a diminishing number of members of the Zvornik Brigade, in the words of the Prosecution, continued to be involved after Pandurevic's return, but there is no evidence that Pandurevic had any contemporaneous knowledge of that. Put rhetorically, if Obrenovic didn't know, which appears to be the case, how could Pandurevic have known? The Prosecution shouts the mantra "must have known" and "needed to know," but we invite you to consider what were the means of Pandurevic's knowledge during these critical hours. There is no evidence in the case that any of the people who might have been able to give him information actually did give him information and that he knew that the elements of the Zvornik Brigade that were involved we now know about. We reiterated the point again that by the 15th of July, we're talking about 15 to 20 soldiers. Look at paragraph 1469. Or, expressed another way, less than 0.4 per cent of the brigade's manpower. That's roughly the equivalent of saying that Mr. Hocking has to know and needs to know what one intern who's here for two weeks is doing on any particular day. The focus of this trial has obviously been on the Zvornik Brigade, since its commander is on trial here. However, one has to place into context that a relatively small number of local conscripts listed as Zvornik Brigade members chose to act as security upon discovering that large numbers of enemy soldiers were being detained in schools close to their homes and that a few local drivers operated machines rather than leave bodies to decompose. Prisoners were taken to Zvornik, guarded on buses, put in schools, without the help of the Zvornik Brigade. Their execution was carried out by military policemen from the Drina Corps and the Bratunac Brigade, soldiers from the 10th Sabotage Detachment, and other unidentified and unidentifiable units. Also, civil authorities took part, and machineries from private companies were being used. Against this backdrop, the sort of involvement you have heard from those few battalion soldiers is peripheral. I'm going to move on now to the drive past Orahovac on the 17th of July, paragraph 1485. The title to this section of the Prosecution brief, in our submission, should be struck out, that there's no evidential basis for suggesting that Pandurevic and Obrenovic drove past Orahovac in the afternoon of the 17th, and whoever drafted this title did so either in complete ignorance of the evidence or in a deliberate attempt to mislead. The only evidence that Pandurevic and Obrenovic were together in the area of Orahovac on the 17th of July comes from the

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President. I was, just before the break, going to deal with the question of the Milici patients at paragraphs 1505 to 1511 of the Prosecution's brief and what I shall call the Sljivancanin point. The Trial Chamber needs to look at care, we submit, at P1309, an intercepted radio communication between General Pandurevic and Cerovic. We say it is plain or at least it is a reasonable inference to draw in Vinko Pandurevic's favour that he, during that conversation, was entitled to believe that the wounded prisoners were being taken to Batkovici, a prisoner exchange camp, and that Cerovic was arranging that. So whether it was Popovic, Cerovic, or somebody else who was overseeing the operation, that is Pandurevic's evidence as to what he thought would happen, so he did, we submit, satisfy himself sufficiently that those prisoners would be afforded the treatment they were entitled to. Add to that, please, the fact that contemporaneously with this, Pandurevic did successfully arrange for all the other prisoners at Standard to go to Batkovic and be exchanged. As a matter of fact, several of those prisoners had been people who escaped executions. Indeed, there was no reason to suppose, during that period of time, that anybody taken prisoner was more or less likely to be a witness of war crimes than anybody else, so the fact that he sent 150 for exchange is an indication that they were all being treated similarly. The intercept is P1309, not P1009. I'm going to move on very swiftly now, please, to the question of effective control of the killing operation in Zvornik. In determining the individual criminal responsibility as well as the command responsibility of the accused on this indictment in relation to the murders in Zvornik, we submit that you're going to have to ask yourselves six questions, from our point of view: Was Beara in Zvornik at the various execution sites? Was Popovic in Zvornik at the various execution sites? Under whose orders were they? What units and what men did they have at their disposal? Were they empowered to give orders to those men and/or units? And did elements of the Zvornik Brigade receive orders from them which they obeyed? It's perhaps inescapable, in such a large piece of work, put together under such pressure, that the Prosecution's brief should show substantial and significant inconsistencies, but it does, and there is no area where it shows more marked inconsistencies than in the way it pleads its case against Vinko Pandurevic, as opposed to the way it pleads its case against the security officers in the dock. To give one classic example, there are two paragraphs which are repeated virtually verbatim but for one critical word. In paragraph 1583, the Pandurevic section, you'll find the Prosecution alleging that in the famous three and a half thousand parcels intercept, Beara is calling Krstic because he needs his authority to take resources for the murder operation, whereas in paragraph 2270, in the section of the brief that pleads the case against Beara, they say that Beara is calling Krstic because he needs merely his assistance. Those two words are far from synonymous. In relation to the section of the case pleaded against Pandurevic, the only piece of evidence which the Prosecution rely on to show that what was going on in Zvornik was an example of the normal operation of the chain of command is that intercept. They rely on nothing else. We submit that that interpretation of that intercept is completely wrong. It doesn't show the operation of a normal chain of command at all. Krstic and Beara are not connected through any normal chain of command. Neither is subordinate or superior to the other. Beara's superior is Tolimir or Mladic, and Krstic's superior is Mladic. The Prosecution agrees with that at paragraph 2260. Krstic's subordinate in the circumstances would be Pandurevic, of course, who is not mentioned by either of them during the course of this conversation at such a critical time. Moreover, Krstic's suggestion that Beara should take units of the Bratunac Brigade or from the MUP indicates no normal chain of command whatsoever. In relation to that, it was Judge Prost who pointed out the quote used a couple of times in the Prosecution's final brief that Beara, Popovic, were doing what they wanted, taking whomever they wanted wherever they wanted, and there is a remarkable echo of that phrase from poor, weak Dragan Jokic in the very text of this intercept. You may think, when Judge Prost put that question to Mr. McCloskey, he rather ducked the issue, but we will come to it more fully now as we analyse the Prosecution's case against Beara and Popovic. I should briefly respond to something Mr. Ostojic said the other day about that intercept. I mean him no harm, but my submission is when his client uttered the words "I have three and a half parcels to distribute," he was there accepting a measure of responsibility which he was taking on. Contrary to the Prosecution's submission in closing, and their final brief, in our submission, makes it can plain that their case against Colonel Beara was that he was in command of a joint task or operation. Without further elaboration, we invite your attention specifically to the following paragraphs of the Prosecution's final brief: 2186, 2223, 2300, 2301, Beara is criminally responsible for planning and instigating the crimes; 2194, he coordinated and oversaw the crimes; 2199, he had a pivotal role in the organisation, coordination and oversight of the JCEs charged in the indictment; 2227, coordination and control of the burial process; 2283, in charge of the operation; 2284, planned and ordered to have the prisoners transferred to Zvornik for detention and execution; 2301, ordered the commission of the crimes for which he is charged in the indictment. If you required any corroboration that those sort of terms, in contemporary Yugoslavian literature, were all command functions, you need look no further than P699, page 13 in the English, points 13, 14, and 15, the definition of command functions. This section of the brief also, we submit, shows the plainest operation of an abnormal chain of command. 2189, 2221, 2223, Beara instructing Momir Nikolic on the 13th of July to go to Zvornik and pass on an order to Drago Nikolic to prepare the transfer of the prisoners, without reference to Pandurevic, Obrenovic, or Blagojevic; 2191, the meeting on the morning of the 14th of July between Beara, Popovic and Drago Nikolic at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters to plan the logistics of the murder operation, again without reference or knowledge of Pandurevic or Obrenovic; 2198, supervising the reburial work of the security officers without the knowledge of Obrenovic; 2252, Beara and Nikolic were both closely involved in the management of the murder operation, and when there were problems with the operations, others looked to them to solve them, again not to Pandurevic; 2253, Beara was working after the Zvornik Brigade headquarters on the morning of the 15th, looking for personnel to execute the prisoners detained at Rocevic and Pilica, without reference to Pandurevic; 2239, 2241, Beara asked PW-104 for assistance with the provision of equipment and machinery, and involved municipal utility companies. I have to slow down. And, lastly, 2301, Beara was relaying or passing on the illegal orders from superiors Mladic and Tolimir to subordinate security officers as well as to the units they engaged to carry out tasks associated with the removal and destruction of the Muslim population. Now, a similar exercise could be carried out in relation to Mr. Popovic, but I won't do so. It's really rather too boring. But on the 10th -- on the 3rd of September of this year, in closing argument, perhaps more lyrically, Mr. Vanderpuye said this in relation to him: "The evidence concerning Bisina shows the elements of the Drina Corps military police over which Mr. Popovic has control, as well as the 10th Sabotage Detachment, were principally involved in carrying out the executions in Bisina. I will note that these same elements were involved in the crimes that were perpetrated at the Branjevo Military Farm on the 16th of July. The only thing that Mr. Popovic was doing in Bisina on the 23rd of July, 1995, as the most senior officer present there, was coordinating, organising, and carrying out orders that he would have received from his commands to execute these men. There is really no other explanation for his presence there, no other explanation. The evidence in this case shows that his knowledge, intent, and conduct were the same concerning the prisoners that were held in the schools in the Zvornik area, the Orahovac school, where he was present on the 14th of July, the Rocevic school, where he was present on the 15th of July, the Kula school, where he was present on the 16th of July. The nature and extent of his involvement in the Bisina executions virtually parallels the circumstances of his presence and participation in the crimes that were committed in Zvornik." Now, this isn't Dragan Jokic talking, this is counsel for the Prosecution, but he might just as well have said on the 14th, 15th and 16th of July, Beara and Popovic were running around taking whomever they wanted wherever they wanted. In relation to Drago Nikolic, the Trial Chamber will wish to ask itself whether he received advance notice of the arrival of the prisoners in Zvornik, a matter about which I think it is specifically alleged my client was lying when he said that is what he was told by Dragan Obrenovic. In order to determine that, we submit, close regard needs to be had to the following pieces of evidence: Firstly, the vehicle work logs relating to the car in which he would have travelled on the 13th and 14th of July, paying multiple visits to the detention sites; secondly, that those schools, and each of them, was ready to receive prisoners before they arrive; and, thirdly, the presence of Zvornik Brigade military policemen who were under his control prior to the arrival of the prisoners at Orahovac and Rocevic. Of course he had advance knowledge that the prisoners were coming. The next question you'll wish to ask yourself is: Who did he tell? In answering that, regard will doubtless be had to the fact that even according to his own theory of command responsibility, he had to tell Obrenovic, and at the time he would have found out, he did find out, at that time he was stuck at the forward command post as a duty officer and needed Obrenovic's permission to leave his post. Of course he told Obrenovic, if only for that reason. Mr. Vanderpuye also told us the other day that the security organs control the military police. With that, we agree, and we have found in this case a body of agreement for that proposition, in spite of the submission of counsel for Drago Nikolic, Pandurevic is not the only person who disagrees with Peter Vuga's opinion on command and control of the military police. PW-168 disagrees with it as well, as did Miodrag Dragutinovic, and they should know, they were the ones who had to operate the system. Peter Vuga did not. We reiterate moreover, our point, our submission, that minute analysis of the Rules is a pointless exercise. Mass murder of prisoners isn't in the rules. It isn't defined as counter-intelligence work, it isn't defined as any sort of work, and you would be better employed looking at who was doing it and who was ordering them to do it. A point is made furthermore at paragraph 1591 of the Prosecution's brief, supported only by the evidence of PW-168, that any orders given by a senior officer present should be reported to the commander of the unit at the first available opportunity. Three brief points which will become the style of these last few minutes, I fear: PW-168 is the only witness who expresses this opinion. Notably, Butler didn't, nor did anybody else who helped command within the VRS. Secondly, PW-168's evidence on this point contradicts Article 17 of the Provisional Service Regulations. And, lastly, in any event, we are dealing with illegal orders in this case. The standard military practice or theory is of limited value. Before I pass on, two short points arising from some remarks of Mr. McCloskey the other day. The suggestion that Beara has or had less authority than Krstic in Zvornik is ridiculous. Beara's special importance to Mladic is highlighted by the Prosecution in paragraph 2183. By contrast, Krstic had only become a commander on the 13th of July. Secondly, as to the Prosecution's glib submission that the difference between the criminal responsibility of commanders and security officers is "immense," that is just historically and jurisprudentially inaccurate. In the Blagojevic case, the Trial Chamber which heard all the evidence sentenced Momir Nikolic, who pleaded guilty and cooperated with the Prosecution, to a much longer term of imprisonment than to his own commander, Blagojevic, who contested his guilt through trial. The use of Zvornik Brigade resources during the period of the executions. Pandurevic gave evidence about which he wasn't challenged that units such as engineering and logistics were effectively self-ordering and that he rarely if ever got involved in how the brigade resources were employed. There is also a body of evidence that shows such organs ran through functional chains of command within the brigade and above, and that's dealt with at paragraphs 238 to 242 of our brief. Whilst, of course, it can't be denied that people who were members of the Zvornik Brigade Engineering Company did drive machines, that is not something ordinarily that Pandurevic would have needed to authorise or would have needed to know about, on the evidence in this case. Significantly, all logistical and engineering equipment was put to use first whilst Obrenovic was in command. That is confirmed by the Prosecution, where it says elements of the Zvornik Brigade continued to take part in the murder operation and after Pandurevic's return; paragraph 1272. There is no evidence that Pandurevic actually knew that any of this machinery was being used or that any of these drivers were employed in this way, other than what he was told by Obrenovic. There is no evidence that Pandurevic spoke to Jokic and was informed by him of any of this at this time. And there is no evidence, in the ordinary course of events, that the brigade commander would know such things. So the repetitive assertion made by the Prosecution about Pandurevic's knowledge and authority is empty. No suggestion of express authority or knowledge was ever put to him. Baljkovica. The Prosecution have not condescended at all to detail about the numbers of casualties, either during this trial or during their investigations. They have left that to us, the Defence. They have left us to show you that the losses were far from spectacular and, in particular, as known to Pandurevic at the time of the opening of the corridor, were scarcely significant. The important or operative number of casualties, you may think, is that which he knew about at the time he chose to open the corridor. Nearly all of the hard evidence about the events of Baljkovica on the 15th and 16th of July were put before the Trial Chamber by the Defence. Although they had it, the Prosecution did not intend for you to hear the taped radio communications between Vinko Pandurevic and Semso Muminovic. It wasn't on their 65 ter list. We had to point out to them that it existed; transcribe it, translate it, and play it for you. It was not us who placed before you the accurate lists -- it was us, not them, who placed before you the accurate lists of deceased, wounded, and missing, and it was us, through our client, not the OTP, through its military analyst, who graphically illustrated to you the disposition of all the VRS forces in the region at Pandurevic's disposal, as well as giving you an insight into the condition of the column by the time of the opening of the corridor. We thought you needed to know these things to judge Pandurevic's motives. The Prosecution didn't want you to know them, and they still, in their brief and oral arguments, urge you to ignore them. The reason is perfectly simple. It damages beyond repair the Prosecution's claims that Pandurevic had genocidal intent, was a member of the JCE to commit mass murder. What is particularly disturbing about the way in which the Prosecution has conducted its case in relation to Baljkovica is the startling failure to put to Pandurevic in cross-examination many of the assertions it now relies upon in its final brief. At the time he took the decision to open the corridor, Pandurevic could only have believed he lost ten men. That is what he wrote in P334, the irregular combat report of the 16th of July. The hearsay and inaccurate estimates of other people listed in paragraph 1597 of the Prosecution brief are irrelevant. Pandurevic was not cross-examined about his beliefs as to the precise number of dead, missing, or wounded. Secondly, Popovic's opinion on what was militarily justifiable is worthless. Apart from anything else, the evidence shows that he never went to Baljkovica on that day. And in our submission, that particular assertion lies ill in the mouth of the Prosecution, who so enjoyed joking with Obrenovic about the unlikelihood of Popovic ever putting himself in the way of a bullet or danger in his interview in 2001. This is the point that the Prosecution can't get 'round, nor do they even attempt to do so: Pandurevic's offer to let the whole column go, soldiers and civilians, was first made on the 15th of July. You heard it. The only thing that stopped everybody being let go before he had even written the report of the 15th of July was a quibble over whether they could take their arms with them. It's on tape. It's 7D656. Richard Butler didn't even want to listen to that tape. The Prosecution didn't want you to know about it because, quite simply, it's the end of their theories about Pandurevic being compelled to let the Prosecution go. Sorry, it's been three years. You have been to Baljkovica. You will remember it is down in a dip, surrounded by hills which represent the forward defence lines of the Zvornik Brigade. The Prosecution's desperate military theory in paragraph 1605 of its brief completely ignores the fact that the point which Pandurevic chose for the Muslims to cross the confrontation line was a really vulnerable one for the Muslim column. It also completely ignores the evidence of both Pandurevic and PW-168 that he could easily have withdrawn his troops a short distance and covered the area with artillery fire, obliterating the whole column. The quote from Pandurevic's irregular combat report of the 16th of July: "I consider Krivaja 95 as not complete as long as a single enemy soldier or civilian remains behind the front-lines," is, of course, ambiguous. The Prosecution, of course, want you to conclude that it is indicative of a pre-existing intention to commit forcible transfer, but bearing in mind, we all agree, that the break-out of the 28th Division towards Nezuk, creating in the process a serious security situation behind Serb lines, was not foreseen by anybody before the commencement of Krivaja 95, it is at least equally possible to construe this sentence as meaning that the security situation had to be tidied up before the operation could be considered to be over. We do, of course, also remind you of the extraordinarily similar conduct of Pandurevic in June 1993, at Ustipraca and the practical manifestations of his relationship with Semso Muminovic, both of which we submit are highly relevant in determining his true motives for allowing the column to pass. These oral arguments won't make it to September. I don't mean September 2009; I mean September 1995. I have had to, to deal with all counts on this indictment, address -- through the evidence and the submission, I mete all forms of criminal liability, and mete 117 pages specifically devoted to my client in the Prosecution's brief. There are, of course, things I've had to leave to one side. I can only hope that if, after all this time, there's something you need my help on, you'll ask me now, because now is the chance. I am not going to say anything more than I've said in my own final brief and which Mr. Josse so eloquently laid out the other day about this being a case in which there's already a pre-existing jurisprudence on sentence, and that the "give them all life" approach is really not helpful to you who might be looking for guidance as to where people fit within the scheme of things, according to the Prosecution, but I will conclude with what I really started with. We invite you, in addition to the events that directly relate to Vinko Pandurevic in July of 1995, to look a bit wider. We invite you to look at Visegrad in April of 1992, to the contact with Semso Muminovic and the cease-fires throughout the whole war, permitting people to grow their crops. We do invite you to look at Kamenica, unashamedly, in January of 1993 and to look at Ustipraca in June of 1993, and to look at the passing of the column, and to look at Silikovic [phoen], the Muslim communications officer; wounds treated, fed and released; the eight boys on the 18th of July at the 4th Battalion command post, released from work and sent back to Semso Muminovic; the 150 prisoners in the prison at Standard whom Vinko Pandurevic secured exchange for at Batkovic. That's probably ineloquently expressed, but you know what I mean. I'm not going to romanticise it by invoking the image of Schindler, as did Mr. McCloskey, but there was something that Vinko Pandurevic said, which I will commend to you, and he said this: "Those who are in my hands survived." And that's true. Those who were in his hands survived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have some questions for you, Mr. Haynes. Judge Prost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Haynes --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You're speaking a bit softly. I better put my headphones on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: I've never been accused of that, Mr. Haynes. First, on the question of command and control, there are various references throughout your brief on this particular issue, but there's one particular question or one particular point I'm not clear on, and it's a statement you make at paragraph 455 in the brief, page 103, and it's, I believe, the only time or at least the only time I could find when you make the statement that as commander of TG-1, Mr. Pandurevic was not the commander of the Zvornik Brigade. And what I'd like to know is -- is your position on that. Specifically, is it your position that at any point from the 4th to the 15th of July, Vinko Pandurevic was not, at law or in fact, the commander of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm looking at the form of that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: I'm not asking about in command, or responsibility, or effective control at this point. I'm asking, squarely: Was he at any point not the commander of the Zvornik Brigade? The way it's framed in that particular paragraph, it references to his other responsibilities at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You're -- in titular sense, you're saying does he ever cease to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: To be the commander of the Zvornik Brigade during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In a titular sense, no. To give a ridiculous example, were he to have gone to a cocktail party, people would have introduced him as the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you. Now moving then to the question of effective control, and here I'm speaking about effective control as it's been defined in the jurisprudence for the purpose of determining the superior/subordinate relationship, in the abstract, to begin with, is it your position -- or what is your position as to whether more than one person can have effective control with respect to the same unit or brigade at a particular point in time?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The simple answer is to that is: Yes, they can. I can't ignore the jurisprudence on that. I've foreshadowed this, I think, briefly in my submission today. Effective control is an evidential question, rather than a legal one, and we do invite you to look very carefully at the effective control of people in the detention/execution areas. But the answer to your question is, no, I'm not submitting for a minute that people, as it were, switched from one to the other permanently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: And then taking the very specific situation, then, Mr. Haynes, with reference to a commander and a deputy commander, is it your position that both a commander and a deputy commander can have effective control over the same unit at the same time? And, again, I appreciate effective control is always a factual, evidentiary determination. Is there anything barring both the deputy commander and the commander having effective control?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Theoretically, there is nothing to prevent that. In practice, I find it hard to imagine an example where it would happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: And we're talking about effective control, not the exercise of effective control, but actual effective control, the material ability that's spoken about --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: -- the in the jurisprudence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Is there any difficulty, then, with both a commander and a deputy commander having effective control in that sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you. And the one final point, and I'm going to take you to the Rule that you've cited with reference to the Prosecution in this case, and that is Rule 90(H)(2).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I don't think we have any further questions for you at this stage, Mr. Haynes. Now, at the beginning of the sitting, we were informed that you would like to address the Chamber, Mr. Bourgon. Very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. We've been informed on Friday that the Prosecution would like to take the floor for about 15 minutes for rebuttal. On behalf of Drago Nikolic, there are three questions I would like to address after that, and these questions are two that were put to me by the Trial Chamber, which I would like to come back to, and the third question arises from a question which was put to the Prosecution earlier on, which is not specifically addressed either in our brief or in our oral arguments I would like to come back to, and that has to do with the nexus. So I would like no more than 15 minutes to address these three questions. And I take this opportunity, Mr. President, to -- I'm not sure if my colleague intends to answer this point, but I raised during my oral arguments, and that was at transcript page 34530, line 20, to 34531, lines 10, the issue of Milici hospital which no longer appears in the Prosecution's pleadings, so I'd like to know, if my colleague does not answer this question, I would like the question to be put to him so that I know where my client, Drago Nikolic, stands regarding Milici hospital. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you're suggesting that you go, if we grant you authorisation, after Mr. McCloskey or before?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: After, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's hear what Mr. McCloskey has to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Given, as you've been reminded, as we all know, it's the Prosecution's burden, the Prosecution should go last in responding to this -- any new evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have roughly 15 minutes left, Mr. Bourgon. The decision is to grant you the request that you have asked, but it's also our decision that you go first, and then we hear what the Prosecution has to say, and, if necessary, consider whether it's the case of asking you -- of allowing you to say anything further. So you will use the next 15 minutes for this purpose. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will move immediately to the first question, which was put to me in private session, so I think we should go into private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sure. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The second question posed to me, Mr. President, had to do with conspiracy, and that was at transcript page 34548. The question related to our temporal limitation argument, and on that day, Mr. President, I said the following: I said that our theory of conspiracy to commit genocide is a continuing crime, and I said that this theory had been rejected by the ICTR. However, what I should have said is that we submit that conspiracy to commit genocide is not a continuing crime on the basis of the ICTR case law, holding that incitement to commit genocide is not a continuing crime. The Appeals Chamber, in Nahimana, held at paragraph 723 that the crime of direct and public incitement to commit genocide was completed as soon as the discourse in question is uttered or published, even though the effects of the incitement may extend in time. It is, therefore, our submission that for the same reason, conspiracy to commit genocide is not a continuing crime. The Zigiranyirazo Trial Chamber - sorry for the pronunciation - considered at paragraph 389 of that judgement that the crime of conspiracy to commit genocide is complete at the moment of agreement, regardless of whether the common objective is ultimately achieved. Similarly, the Musema Trial Chamber held at paragraph 194 that the crime of conspiracy to commit genocide is punishable, even if it fails to produce a result. The Prosecution alleges in this case that the agreement to commit genocide would have been concluded on 11 or 12 July in Bratunac. That is paragraph 34 of the indictment, and that the mass killings commence on 13 July. That is paragraph 30 of the indictment. This means the conspiracy to commit genocide was completed on 11 and 12 July and that the genocide would have commenced on 13 July. It is therefore the Defence's position that on the basis of the ICTR case law, the conspiracy to commit genocide would have been completed on 11-12 July and that the situation thereafter is regulated by the law relative or relating to genocide. Consequently, anyone allegedly involved in the crimes committed after the conclusion of the agreement to commit genocide on 11 and 12 July could possibly incur liability for the crime of genocide, provided, of course, that all relevant conditions have been met, but not for the crime of conspiracy to commit genocide. Finally, it is not excluded that the example given by Judge Prost of Judges Stole and Kwon joining a conspiracy, concluded by Judge Prost and Judge Agius, could result in liability for conspiracy for Judges Stole and Kwon if the criminal activity has not commenced prior to Judges Stole and Kwon joining the conspiracy. However, if the criminal activity has commenced, we submit that in this particular example, Judge Stole and Kwon cannot join the conspiracy, but rather their conduct would be regulated by the law relating to the criminal activity that would have been committed in such an example. I move quickly, Mr. President, to the last question, which is the one that was asked to the Prosecution in two places at transcript 34261 and transcript 34288, relating to the nexus which is required between the military column and the attack on Srebrenica within the concept of crimes against humanity and the "chapeau" requirements. Our position in this regard is the following: First, we acknowledge the decision of the Appeals Chamber that crimes against humanity generally can be committed against combatants "hors de combat," or, in other words, combatants "hors de combat" can be victims of crimes against humanity, but that's only the beginning and part of the argument. The underlying crime must be committed, of course; in this case, forcible transfer. In the absence of any specific allegations in this regard, if we talk about forcible transfer, lex specialis which applies is IHL, International Humanitarian Law, and that would be Article 49 of Geneva Convention 4 and not Common Article 3, as mentioned by my colleague from the Prosecution. This fits in the economy of Article 5 of the Statute, which requires that an attack be directed at any civilian population. Hence, even if the Trial Chamber was to find that forcible transfer can be committed against prisoners of war, for the purpose of crimes against humanity two additional requirements must be filled: First, the commission of an act which, by its nature or consequences, is objectively part of the attack, and this must be coupled with, of course, knowledge on the part of the accused that there is an attack on the civilian population and that his acts, or parts there of, if the accused does not have both the knowledge of the attack directed against the civilian population and the knowledge that his acts are part of this attack, then he cannot be found guilty of a crime against humanity. In Mrksic, the Appeals Chamber said that the fact that the perpetrators of the crime acted in the understanding that the victims of the crimes were selected both on their perceived involvement in the Croatian armed forces and, as such, were treated differently from the civilian population, precludes that they intended that their acts form part of the attack against the civilian population of Vukovar, and this rendered their acts so removed from the attack that no nexus can be established; paragraph 42. We believe --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm just trying to fit within the 15 minutes, and I'm almost done. I apologise. We believe that the situation in this case concerning the men from the column, on one example, and also the men separated at Potocari, which is another example, but that in both cases these men were also treated differently from the local population. In our submission, they were legitimately transported as prisoners of war to detention facilities. And the evidence, of course, shows that the attacks directed at the column was legitimate because the attackers acted in the understanding that they were engaging members of the ABiH, or combatants, or civilians who directly participated in the hostilities, which is the part that was already covered in our brief, so I'm not going to expand on that. But the thing that the attack could have been attack lawfully, it is incorrect for the Prosecution to talk about a grey area today. The column was a legitimate attack, and the attackers, when they attacked the column, they were not attacking or doing acts which form part of the attack against the civilian population of Srebrenica, which the Prosecution acknowledge in responding to the Trial Chamber's question, began much earlier and dealt with something completely different from the column retreating and being engaged. The lex specialis again which applies in such circumstances is the law of armed conflict or IHL, and the fact that the column could have been attacked lawfully precludes the qualification of these acts as crimes against humanity. I could -- I had more, but I'll stop here, Mr. President. I think I made the point that I wanted to make. The last thing I can add is: There are -- the understanding of those who attacked the column is one thing. The understanding of those who separate the men in Potocari is a second thing. But what is important for our client is the fact that Drago Nikolic, when he is in the Zvornik area, the information that he has is about prisoners of war and nothing about that this would be part of the attack on the civilian population of Srebrenica. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. McCloskey, what's your forecast for tomorrow, now that you have just heard Mr. Haynes and Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I hope not to take more than 15 minutes for two different responses, to Pandurevic and to Borovcanin. I will review everything again, try to get it down to the essence, and I would hope no more than 30 minutes. I don't think I have more than 30 minutes left in me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. And that means, Mr. Krgovic, Mr. Josse, and Ms. Nikolic, Mr. Bourgon, please, your clients will be expected to make their statements tomorrow. Okay. You may agree amongst yourselves who goes -- who goes first. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. There are also a small number of corrections from Friday's transcript which I'd like to make tomorrow, if I may, please. It will take no time at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. That applies to everyone. Thank you. We'll stand adjourned to tomorrow morning at -- tomorrow is in the afternoon at quarter past 2.00. Thank you.
